titleStmt.title: Liber de natura rerum, versions I-II

sourceDesc.p: Traduction anglaise auto-generee (IA, non relue par un latiniste) a partir du texte latin du corpus zoomathia sous zoo66/1l (Thomas Cantimpratensis, Liber de natura rerum, versions I-II, edition Mattia Cipriani / Emmanuelle Kuhry, IRHT). SEUL LE LIVRE 4 "De animalibus quadrupedibus" (animaux quadrupedes, 113 chapitres + 1 prologue, 493 citations) est traduit pour le moment ; il s'agit d'un premier jalon. Les livres 5 "De avibus" (oiseaux, 341 citations), 6 "De monstris marinis" (93 citations), 7 "De piscibus" (172 citations), 8 "De serpentibus" (128 citations) et 9 "De vermibus" (120 citations) restent a traduire (total de l'oeuvre : 1347 citations). La structure du div (oeuvre > section1 livre [n=4] > section2 prologue/chapitre > cit avec <bibl> d'attribution et <quote>) est integralement preservee ; les notes d'identification savante de l'editeur (Mattia Cipriani), qui ne font pas partie du texte de Thomas lui-meme, ont ete exclues de la traduction, de meme que pour l'extraction du texte latin source. A distinguer de zoo66/2e, qui traduit une version differente de l'oeuvre (dite "Thomas III" / zoo66/2l). Traduction fournie a titre de meilleur effort ; a verifier par un latiniste avant toute citation savante. Correspond au texte latin deja present dans le corpus sous zoo66/1l (source Sourcencyme/IRHT).

cit.quote: In general, concerning quadrupeds: Ass, Wild boar, Domestic boar, Aloy, Anabulla, Elk, Ahanes, Ana, Buffalo, Bonasus, Camel, Dog, Beaver, Cama, Calopus, Camelopard, Goat, Roe deer, Cat, Cefusa, Stag, Chimera, Cyrogrillus, Rabbit, Hamster, Corocrotta, Catoblepas, Demma, Dammula, Duran, Badger, Elephant, Horse, Equicervus, Eale, Henichires, Hemtra, Hedgehog, Ermine, Falena, Ferret, Furio, Marten, Finge, Dormouse, Genet, Genetha, Guesseles, Ibex, Hybrid, Porcupine, Hyena, Lion, Leopard, Lamia beast, Lanzani, Lynx, Wolf-dog, Wolf, Leucrocota, Leoncophona, Hare, Lachta, Otter, Locust-beast, Mule, Unicorn, Mastiff, Mauricomorion, Manticore, Musk-deer, Mammonet, Shrew, Cat, Weasel, Mouse and its kinds, Ichneumon, Wild ass, Indian wild ass, Onocentaur, Oryx, Oraflus, Sheep, Panther, Panther, Reindeer, Pegasus, Pilosus, Pathio, Polecat, Pyrolus, Rangifer, Ape, Tiger, Bull, Indian bull, Tranez, Tragelaph, Troglodyte, Mole, Unicorn, Bear, Vesontes, Aurochs, Fox, Varius, Zubrones, Zybo. Here end the chapters. Here begins the fourth book, on quadrupeds.

Aristotle: First it must be said in general concerning the four-footed animals. Aristotle: animals that have two feet or four or none have blood; but those that have more than four feet do not have blood, and this is understood of the blood that is arranged through veins. But worms do not have blood in veins - like lice and fleas - for they lack veins.

Pliny: it is a general rule that all marine animals have bony eyes and tough skin; and this is because the salt water would otherwise penetrate what is delicate and soft, and they could not survive unless nature had made them stronger than other creatures. And in this it is noted that worldly men have a hardened understanding toward spiritual things, because the salt of wisdom cannot penetrate them.

Aristotle: every animal that has ears has them mobile, except man; and rightly so, because he ought to hold God's commandments fixed in his heart. Whence it is said to him: "Write them as on the tablet of your heart." Some hearing animals do not have ears but openings, as every winged creature and every scaly one; and in this the forgetful are reproved. Whence it is said in the common speech: the word enters one ear of the fool and goes out the other. All animals move the lower jaw except the crocodile and the centelia, which move the upper. The tongue is the instrument of taste, and that sense is only at its tip. The tongue perceives what is common to the whole body, such as heat, cold, hardness, softness; and it does this through all its parts. The tongue is either narrow or broad, but the middling kind is more praiseworthy, for it is better suited to the goodness of motion. Therefore do not be diffuse in words, for in much speaking sin will not be lacking; nor mute, for such are called dogs unable to bark. This is sometimes free, sometimes hindered, and this happens either from bad habit or from bad disposition, as happens with the tongue-tied.
they approach man's proportion in size more than in other animals.

Let understanding and affection be joined in us, that is knowledge of ourselves and knowledge of God, that they may be to us as two eyes by which we are led into heaven. Of these it is said in the Song of Songs: "Your two eyes are like the pools in Heshbon," etc.

Ambrose: to some beasts the Lord gave longer and more extended necks, such as horses, camels, and elephants; to some he gave narrower and shorter necks, such as lions and tigers. Is it not an evident cause, that for those wild beasts which live on flesh there was no need of a long neck? For they do not bend their necks and mouths to the ground to graze, but attack a stag or a bull or tear apart a sheep. So too those who live by the plunder of the poor cannot have length of hope: for how can they hope for a merciful God who are cruel toward the poor? Mercy is for him alone who shows no mercy. But the camel, being taller, how could it feed on the smallest herbs unless it stretched its long neck down to the ground for the purpose of grazing? And so the camel, in proportion to its height, was given a longer neck, the horse for the same reason, and likewise the ox: for these feed on grasses. Almost all ruminant animals have a long neck, and in this it is signified that those who gladly ruminate the divine Scriptures are more easily raised up to hope. All animals that live in water and have teeth have close-set and sharp teeth, so that they may cut quickly and pass their food into the stomach easily without delay, lest the flow of the waters carry off and dissolve their food from between their teeth. Hence fish do not ruminate; only the scarus fish is excepted, which is said to ruminate.

the ox and the sheep and many other animals have teeth on only one side, and yet both jaws are armed with teeth, because it was not necessary, since they ruminate and chew with deliberation and send their food to the interior. So too those who wish to arrive at fruitful knowledge ought to ruminate long in their meditations on the understanding of Sacred Scripture, so that from it they may draw out something they can imitate. Nor should those be reckoned worthy who, like the fish that quickly swallows the food it seizes, do not ruminate and afterward forget to trouble themselves with imitating it. Aristotle: every animal having blood has a brain. Every animal having a hairy tail has a small head and large jaws. And alas, how true this is today of those who rule over men and households, who have hairy - that is, superfluous - tails, in that they are small of head and diminished in their senses, and have large jaws, because they keep many who consume superfluously what should be used to sustain the poor. Hair on animals and wool on sheep vary according to the situation of places and lands: in a hot land they are curly and coarse, in a cold land hanging and soft. Only man's hair turns white in old age. Every four-footed animal that has horns lacks upper teeth and has four stomachs. But an animal without horns has only one stomach, like man and the lion and other animals. Hairs arise from superfluities; so from superfluity of food arises superfluity of humors. Every animal of much fat has little seed. Nor is it a wonder, then, if those who are fattened with the grease of iniquity or fattened with delights or thickened with temporal things are found to have little seed of good works; whence: "My beloved grew fat and kicked." And it is to be noted that blood is the natural moisture always remaining in those that have blood, and there is no vital blood except in the veins and the heart. Its taste is sweet and its color red, unless it is corrupted. No animal of good disposition has much seed. Every animal, as Aristotle says, that has many hairs, and every bird having many feathers, has much seed and much mating. By seed a word spoken is sometimes signified. No wonder, then, that idle words are as seed; whence: "You have sown much, and brought in little." The more fat increases, the more blood diminishes; nor is it a wonder, for "the yoke [of sin] rots away before the oil [of grace]." A body having much blood putrefies more quickly; whence: "The beasts rotted in their own dung." Rennet is found in the stomach of suckling and ruminating animals, and the older it grows, the better it is, and it is effective against flux of the bowels, especially that of the hare and the stag. Rightly, therefore, do those who often ruminate the Scriptures for the edification of their neighbor through preaching have ready the sweetness of doctrine. Whence, conversely, rennet is not found in the stomach of non-ruminating animals. Every hairy animal has viscous seed. For those who live often amid delights cannot have pure works. A man having much hair in the beard and on the pubis generates more quickly, especially if it is black in color. Every animal having blood walks, wakes, and sleeps; and every animal having eyelids closes them in sleep, except the hare and the lion. By the eyelids is understood discretion of judgment, and this is frequently closed and darkened in the sleep of sin. The foods of animals vary according to the matter from which they come, since growth in all things comes only from that in which they naturally delight. And indeed they differ among themselves, for some are land-dwelling, some marine; one must preach differently to religious, differently to seculars, differently to laymen, and differently to lettered seculars. Whence the faithful servant is praised in this, that he gives food at the proper time. Every footed animal can naturally swim for a time. Man, however, is naturally less able than any animal, and this is because of the gall bladder, which he has less of than all animals in proportion to the size of his body. Fish, however, are more able, because they have a larger gall bladder in proportion to their body's size.

For the body consists of four humors, bearing forth the qualities of the four elements. That humor which has received a fiery nature and a hot and dry property is conceived, enclosed, and retained in the gall. And what is hot and dry must necessarily be light. And what is naturally light, unless kept enclosed, necessarily tends upward. Whence it happens that when a man sinks in water, he soon touches bottom; but after a few days he floats upon the water. For while the aforesaid gall-bladder holds the lightness of the body enclosed, it cannot raise the limbs. But when, the container having burst, it is diffused through the limbs, it is an effective cause, by qualitative necessity, of being carried upward and poorly raising its own limbs. Though this reasoning cannot be contradicted, neither can it be proven. We believe the possibility of swimming in fish comes rather from a bladder filled with air than from the gall. It is also a rather amusing question, why the boar has tusks, the lion claws, the bull horns, by which they avoid dangers; while others, like roe deer, does, or hares, preserve their being by the lightness of flight: yet man, worthier than all of these, has none of this. And it is resolved thus: man indeed, being a rational and therefore social animal, is fit for two activities, namely action and counsel. Daily experience teaches that in matters of war the use of arms is required; in time of peace, the same must be laid aside. If, then, man had arms innate to himself, when negotiating the covenants of peace he would not be able to lay them aside. Likewise, if he were fortified with lightness of flight, he would lose steadiness by his wandering, and by the unfitness of his slender limbs would be found feeble when weakness came upon him. But as it is, when there is need he takes up arms, and when peace requires it he lays them down again, and when he needs to be swift he can, through the skill of vehicles, and when the necessity is removed he is taught to return to steadiness. Thus, then, the question is resolved, why the bull and not man has horns.

Aristotle: all land creatures that breathe and generate their like have a windpipe, through which they draw water [air], and a lung, by which they draw air. Through the windpipe we draw the grace of God through desire; through the lung we breathe toward heavenly things through hope. Every wild animal having a saw-like row of teeth eats flesh; and in this it is signified that every prince surrounded by cruel ministers preys upon the poor. And every animal having saw-like teeth draws water with its tongue. So too every preacher ought to draw the grace of both God and men in preaching. But animals that have even teeth draw water into their stomach by sucking. So too those who have continual prayers attain the grace of contemplation. Animals that have many teeth are, in most cases, long-lived; but those with few teeth are short-lived. Every animal lacking a lung lacks a voice, but the converse does not hold. For those who are not raised up to heaven by hope cannot open their mouth in prayer: for what would they ask for that they did not hope for? No animal ejects seed outside the female vessel, whether waking or sleeping, except man; and in this man is most wretched and most shameful, for even if sleeping he does so without will, yet waking, with the judgment of his own will, he is polluted and defiled by exceeding into every wickedness. The growth of all animals lies in that in which they naturally delight. And what or who delights us but our one best God? And he himself is the delight of the upright of heart, and all things naturally seek delight: the miser delights in money, the lustful in luxury. And animals vary according to the places in which they dwell. What wonder? "With the holy you shall be holy." For example, pigs that live in cold places have flattened and drooping hair, and stiff; but pigs that live in warm places are curly, and have black hair, curling over the whole body. All animals that ruminate are much helped and improved by the fact that they ruminate, because they sense in it a certain sweetness; and these animals are fattened more quickly on little food than animals that do not ruminate at all, and this is from the very delight of rumination. No wonder, since according to Solomon, "the soul that blesses [God, in its prayers] shall be made fat, and he who gives drink shall himself also be given drink." All animals are of a hard nature like trees, since their head is, as it were, in place of the root, and because of this it happens that their upper limbs are below and their lower limbs above. Whence man is called an inverted tree: the head with its hair is its roots. This root of the head draws in nourishment, whence the limbs live. So in the soul the head, that is the root, is the mind, the branches are the virtues, the mouth is the desire of the heart, whence all the virtues receive nourishment. Every animal that has blood and four feet has four stomachs: the first stomach receives raw food, the second receives it digested, the third carries the food received to a better digestion, the fourth receives the food well digested and releases it. Every animal lacking gall lives long, like the elephant, the stag, the camel, and the dolphin. No wonder, since the Lord says: "The meek shall inherit the earth," and what land but that of the living? Some animals have five toes on the front feet and four on the hind, like the lion, the dog, and the wolf; some animals have five toes on the hind feet, so that their motion may be lighter and swifter. We ought to have the affection of love, as it were five toes on our feet: toward God, toward ourselves, toward our neighbor, toward friend and toward enemy. Every four-footed animal has a tail, because the soul, founded on the four cardinal virtues, is brought to a good end. Man, however, has no tail, but has hips, that is buttocks, in place of a tail, and what passes into the tail in other beasts passes into the hips in him. And the same reasoning applies to the bear or the ape, which have no tail, since they have hips like man. Nature placed the tail to cover the outlet of digestion; and charity, in the end, covers a multitude of sins. This, then, the hips do that the tail does.

cit.quote: As the great Basil says: the soul of brute beasts is blood. But congealed blood is wont to be turned into flesh, and corrupted flesh returns to earth. Rightly, then, is the soul of beasts of burden a fading thing. See then the sequence: soul to blood, blood to flesh, flesh to earth; and again, resolving these by retracing the same path, that is from earth to flesh, from flesh to blood, from blood to soul, and you will find that the spirit of beasts is earth.

Animals of large body are of small fertility, and those of small body of great; and the reason is that necessarily much is dissolved in animals of large body, and little is left over. And alas, how true we see this to be today, that those who seem greater in dignity bear little fruit; and the reason is that "a mind intent on many things is diminished as to each single one." Every animal that devours its food, like the lion or the wolf, is of a lean body, because where there is no chewing of food, the food passes badly into the animal's nature. The heavier beasts all feed on grain, the more agile on flesh, like lions and wolves. Before the Flood, men fed only on grain. Therefore, according to the saying of the wise man, let man, by the fruit of his labors, feed as it were on grain, while the predatory lion feeds on flesh - and who is this but the noble prince who is a predator, living off the labors of the poor?

Man is surpassed in the five senses by many creatures: eagles and lynxes see more clearly, vultures smell more keenly, (the ape tastes more subtly, the spider feels more quickly); moles (or the wild boar) hear more acutely: "The boar surpasses us in hearing, the lynx in sight, the ape in taste, the vulture in smell, the spider in touch." Some animals, as Pliny says, are naturally bald, like the ostrich, camels, and water-ravens. For he is not truly rich who is not stripped of his superfluities in death, and this naturally, because the dead man knows not how to be a possessor. The insatiable among animals are those from whose stomach food passes straight through, like wolves, stags, and, among birds, gulls and the pelican. By this are signified forgetful students or hearers of the divine law, who always wish to hear and store up nothing in the stomach of memory for doing good. Man has eight ribs, and some ten; horned animals thirteen; serpents thirty. In all animals, as Pliny says, of whatever kind one is found gentle, of the same kind a wild one is also found, just as among men too so many kinds of wild men are found,
such as satyrs, onocentaurs, and other kinds, of which the blessed Jerome writes.

Accordingly, as Isidore says: human industry has forced diverse animals together in mating, and thus by adulterous mixture has found another kind, just as Jacob, contrary to nature, produced likenesses of colors. For his ewes conceived offspring such as the shadows of the rams mounting above, which they beheld reflected in the water. Indeed this same thing is said to happen among herds of horses, that they set noble-looking horses before the eyes of the mares as they conceive, so that they may conceive offspring resembling them. Hence it is that some order pregnant women to look upon no very ugly faces of animals, such as baboons or apes, lest, meeting their eyes, they bear similar offspring. For they say this is the nature of women, that whatever they have looked upon or conceived in their mind at the height of pleasure's heat, while they conceive, they produce such offspring. For indeed the animal, in the act of mating, transmits inwardly the forms seen from without, and, having its fill of their impressions, seizes their likeness into its own quality.
Whence Aristotle says that a woman lay with an Ethiopian and bore a white daughter, and that white daughter afterward bore an Ethiopian daughter, though not by an Ethiopian.

Those with longer lifespans are carried longer [in the womb], as Pliny says. Those with solid hooves bear single young, those with cloven hooves twins. Those whose toes are divided by a cleft bear more numerous young. But all the former bring forth their young fully formed, the latter incomplete, as is the case with the lioness, the fox, and the she-bear.
It may be asked why some animals ruminate. Solution: fire has a certain property, that it dissolves what is joined together; animals, therefore, that have a hot stomach, cook their food easily.

For there is no delay, as Gregory says in teaching, where the Holy Spirit, the teacher, is present: for the Spirit searches even the depths of the heart, and he himself is the spirit of understanding.

But animals that are of a cold nature, when they take food, are unable to cook it because of the defect of their constitution; whence it happens that they call it back to the teeth, so that, ground a second time there, the food may more easily be able to be softened (and, once softened, be digested). It is plain, then, that oxen, stags, and similar animals of this kind are of a colder nature. These animals, moreover, have a dry and harder and more solid fat than others.

Animals of this kind signify lukewarm and cold students, who, because they are not fervent in spirit, can grasp the secrets of Sacred Scripture only with difficulty, because wisdom will not enter into a malicious soul - especially that which is called savory wisdom - nor dwell in a body enslaved to sins. These have a harder and dry fat, that is, sweetness without devotion. Such fall to the ground first from the hind part, because, forgetful of future goods, they gape after earthly things. Whence, when Moses invited his father-in-law Jethro to go with them because the Lord had promised good things to Israel, he refused, but returned to Midian, that is, to strife or to judgment. For such men seek honors and high seats, and therefore the Lord will dispute with them in the valley of Jehoshaphat, that is, the judgment of the Lord. Such men, indeed, when returning to their heart, ought to rise from the front part first, and, stretched forward, ought to forget the things behind.

But the warmer animals - like the pig and the sheep - have a softer and more thoroughly cooked fat. Yet the sheep, which is of a warm nature, ruminates, but this is because it lacks efficacy of teeth, whence they are called "bidents." It may again be asked why ruminant animals with suet lie down first on the hind part. Solution: indeed the limbs of such animals are not equally cold; for there is more cold in the hind parts, and this for the reason that those parts are farther from the heart; therefore where there is greater cold, there must necessarily be greater heaviness. Rightly, then, do they lie down on the heavier part first. But they ought to rise first from the front part, because that place is warmer, and nearer to the fire of the heart; and fire always tends upward. It may again be asked why some animals see better by night than by day. Solution: in the eye, which is the instrument of sight, there are several humors. One white, (bright and clear), through which the visible spirit is diffused; the other black, through which care is taken (that the white and bright humor not be too much dispersed). Those animals, then, that see less by day abound in the whitest humor; whence it happens that the spirit is more diffused, and by reason of this diffusion they lose discrimination of what is to be seen by day; but by night, because of the darkness, the spirit is gathered together, and so a greater discrimination results. For when we wish to see something with discernment, we contract our eyebrows, so that the gathered spirit of the eye does not wander.

As the great Basil says: to sheep and goats and very many other living things a natural sense is given of avoiding what is harmful among plants; only to men, who discern by understanding, is the skill of the medical art available, and yet the frequent experience of harmful things is very difficult even for them.

The ass, as the Book of Properties says, is an unshapely animal, vile and despised, with a great head, broad and long ears beyond a cubit's measure, a lean body, unable to grow fat. On its shoulders it bears the marks of Christ's cross, and rightly so, for Christ, hastening to his passion to redeem the world by death, sat upon its humble, poor, and gentle back. And so the ass is an animal that knows no discord, a friend of peace, gentle, patient, and most enduring under blows, a bearer of burdens, not rebelling against the loads placed upon it, even beyond what it can carry. These are its good natural qualities. But its vices are these: the ass is a lustful animal, stronger and more powerful in its hindquarters than in its forequarters (for it carries its load behind), slow and sluggish in gait, brutish and irrational beyond all living things, and going along the road it does not know how to give way to one it meets, and is horrible in its braying.

The foals of asses have some comeliness in their youth, but the older they grow, the uglier they become. The ass mates after thirty months, but does not breed until after three years. The milk of the she-ass, as Pliny says, is the whitest, and is thought to lend some brightness to the skin. Whence it is found that Poppaea, Nero's wife, used to bathe herself in the milk of she-asses.

As the Experimentator says, asses for the most part fall ill on one side, having a discharge; if it flows from the nostrils inward and settles on the lung, the animal dies. The flesh of asses, when eaten, generates very bad blood and is digested with difficulty; yet it is finer than the flesh of horses.

As the Book of Kyranides says, if you make a ring from an ass's hoof and give it to a demoniac to wear, he will be freed that same day. Its tear, mixed and shaken with oil, and put in a lamp and lit, all those at the banquet will see themselves as having asses' heads.
The ass gladly eats thorns.
Warm ass's milk strengthens the teeth and eases their pains (especially if they are rubbed with it).

It also relieves sighing complaints. If you place a she-ass beside her foal and then remove her, keeping the foal from following, the foal will remain in the place where its mother left it and will not move a step further, but will wait for its mother in the place where she left it. The ass is a very cold animal, and for this reason asses are not born in cold places, since its nature cannot bear excessive cold, especially at the time of conception. Whence in the region called Scotland, and in its neighboring and similar regions such as Pontus, the she-ass does not conceive nor is the ass bred. For this reason asses do not mate at the equinox, the time when horses mate, but in summer, so that the birth and generation of the offspring may occur in warm weather. They carry the young in the womb for a full year. In the land of the North, which is the coldest of all inhabitable lands, the ass is not found because of the excessive cold, since they cannot live there.

The bones of asses, as Pliny says, are more resonant than those of other animals. The she-ass rarely bears twins. When about to give birth, she flees the light and seeks darkness, lest she be seen by man - and this is what the Lord commands: "Let not your left hand know what your right hand does." She bears young her whole life, which for her lasts to thirty years. O truly blessed are they whose life, persevering without fault of sin, has brought the fruit of good works to perfection in innocence: for "he who perseveres to the end shall be saved." Through fires they make their way to their young: "No one has greater love than this, that he lay down his life for his friends." And in this the sluggishness of prelates is reproved, who are unwilling to endure even a small tribulation for their subjects, and thereby prove themselves hirelings. If a stream lies in their way, they dread utterly to touch it with their feet. They will drink from no springs but those they are accustomed to, and only the best: blessed are they who, when thirsty, come to Christ and drink, that living waters may flow from them through preaching. But now, O cleric, who gape after riches and delights, answer Jeremiah when he asks; for he says in the second chapter: "And now what have you to do with the way of Egypt, that you should drink the water of the Nile? And what have you to do with the way of Assyria, that you should drink the water of the river?" The muddy water of Egypt, which is interpreted as darkness, is worldly learning, such as the arts and civil law, by which Christ the truth can neither be known nor censured of itself. But the water of the river of the Assyrians is the anxious care of those who gather fleeting and perishable riches, and who, given over to gluttony through these, apply themselves daily to draining their cups. Asses, if they see across the middle of a river, do not easily cross.

The wild boar, as the Book of Properties says, is a strong beast, which never receives any training in good conduct, but is always savage and fierce. It is black in color. It has large and curved tusks, half a foot long, fit for cutting. But this is quite marvelous about its tusks: in the living beast they can do what iron does, but once removed from the dead beast they are proven to have lost their cutting power. By the wild boar certain fierce men of the world may be signified, who, in the letter, receive no training in good works, but are always savage and fierce, black, that is, foul and wicked, in their conduct, as is judged. They have curved tusks in themselves, because he who harms another first wounds himself in conscience by his evil intent. It has tusks of half a foot, because though they wound the body, they have no power over the soul. And this is fitting in such men: while they live, they can only rage; but once dead and cast down into hell, their tyranny ceases. This animal, if attacked by hunters in the morning before it has voided its urine, is easily wearied. But if it has passed urine before or during the hunt, it yields to capture only with difficulty; and even when tired it does not give way, for it holds firm on its hindquarters and, with rigid fierceness, conceals its weariness, offering combat to the hunter. Yet it does not presume to strike or attack a man unless it has first received a blow from him. Therefore let a man take good care of himself, for unless with the first thrust of his spear-point he deals a mortal wound between the shoulder and the flank, his life may be in peril, unless perhaps he finds nearby a tree to climb to for refuge, or in a lower place presses his whole body flat against the ground; even so, he will have to endure the trampling of its feet, until someone nearby comes to help him as he lies there. For its opposed and curved tusks, as we have said, serve as weapons capable of dealing the most savage death, yet they cannot reach anyone but one standing upright and raised. It flees into the brambles, so that the dogs which pursue it, even holding it by the teeth, may be shaken off.
The wild boar surpasses all beasts in hearing.
The males, as Pliny says, are extremely fierce in mating, the females fiercer in giving birth; and this is nearly the same in almost every kind of beast.

As the Experimentator says, the fresh, warm dung of the wild boar is an excellent remedy against bleeding from the nose. The boar has, on its right side, a mouth-like structure shaped like a shield, and turns this to face hunting-spears and weapons. Pierced through by spear or sword, it advances against its attacker along the lance itself. As the aforesaid author says, pork is cold and moist in nature, and this especially of the domestic kind; suckling pig is even more moist and turns into various and putrid humors, especially if it finds a poorly disposed stomach. If a sow eats many acorns while pregnant, she will miscarry. It is proper to pigs to seek their food by rooting up the ground and to wallow snout-first in mud and filth. A sow's first litter will be smaller and weaker than her later litters. When she has many young, her milk is then very scant. In warm regions the offspring of a sow is better in winter than in summer; in cold regions the reverse; and this is because of the intemperate nature of the regions. In India the tusks of wild boars curve to the length of a cubit. There are also wild boars from whose foreheads horns grow like those of calves. But in Arabia the pig kind does not live.

div.head: 4. De apro domestico vel porco vel sue

cit.quote: The domestic boar, as the Book of Properties says, is likewise a savage and unclean beast, which most gladly dwells in filthy and muddy places, and, once washed, does not long refrain from wallowing again in such places. Among domestic boars, one always prevails by strength and rules over the rest; but if a stronger one comes upon him, he attacks the former ruler in combat and strives by his strength to obtain victory; and without delay, the vanquished yielding, the victor rules over the rest. At the squeal of one, the whole herd of pigs, rushing from every side, is roused to a frenzy.

It is dangerous to come upon them in their anger. They say that sows, as Pliny states, become so fierce in mating that they tear at a man, especially one dressed in white clothing: their very rage is calmed when vinegar is naturally sprinkled on them. The males do not breed past three years of age. The females are castrated with their mane cut off, and thus fatten more quickly. Having lost one eye, a pig dies more quickly.

The lifespan of pigs, as Aristotle says, is fifteen years. Pigs suffer from a disease called 'brancos,' which frequently occurs in the ear, or in the foot, or the tail, or in some other part of the body, though rarely. From this disease the flesh in that place is corrupted, and the corruption gradually spreads to the neighboring flesh, until, through the swelling of some vein, it reaches the lung, and then the animal dies. And this disease increases suddenly. Shepherds who recognize this disease should immediately cut off the affected limb. This disease occurs frequently when the heat is great. [A variant account, with the same content, follows in the source under a different siglum.]

Flux of the bowels is not remedied in the pig. The pig eats serpents, and is fattened on roots. When the boar solicits the female, she holds her ears stiff, and does not yield until he has released them. The pig fattens more quickly than other animals; the wild boar within six days. A fourth part of the pig's food turns into hair, blood, and the like. When the sow gives birth, she grows thin. The male pig mates until the age of three years, beginning at seven months, but at so tender an age produces weak offspring. The sow conceives for fifteen years. The male pig has great capacity for mating compared to other animals, provided he is fat. When the sow has given birth, she gives the first teat to the first-born. The worst sows are those that tear apart their own newborn young.
Pork in summer, after the spring season, is harmful to eat right up until after the autumn equinox, because in warm weather the pig sleeps more than suits its nature.

For excess of sleep produces corruption. And it gapes so much after sleep, especially the weak pig, that unless it is roused meanwhile, it will die as if of a lethargic sleep. As the moon wanes toward its last quarter, the brain in the pig is said to shrink more than in any other animal, and this to such a degree that, in proportion to the body, only a small part remains.

The aloy is an animal nearly similar to a mule, whose knees cannot bend like an elephant's. For this reason it does not lie down to sleep, but leans against a tree, which tree, being nearly ready to fall, is cut by hunters, and while the animal leans on its accustomed support, it falls to ruin along with the tree. Thus it is captured; otherwise it is difficult to take, for in that rigidity of its hocks it possesses an unstoppable speed of flight.

The anabulla, as Pliny writes, is a beast of Ethiopia. This animal has a neck like a horse's, feet and legs like an ox's, a head like a camel's. It has white spots, its individual limbs marked with a deep reddish color.
Since, then, this animal is adorned with such beauty, its very striking hide is sold at a high price; and this feeds the luxury of the eyes, which are scarcely ever healed of their beastly curiosity.
The elk, as Solinus says, is an animal in every way similar to a mule, except that it has an upper lip so extended that, unless it walks backward, that is goes in reverse, it cannot graze on grass.

This signifies certain dialecticians of this age, who, being too eager to hear the arts, neglect grammar. Let such men know, then, that if they wish to be nourished by true knowledge, they must go back to the first foundation of grammar. Or it signifies also those who, eager for contemplation, forget and do not mourn their sins; whence: "I trust in the Lord; how then do you say to my soul, Flee to the mountain like a sparrow?" And it follows: "For behold, the sinners [that is, the demons] have bent their bow," etc.

The ahane is an animal, as Aristotle says, the size of a stag, in which nature has changed the custom of other quadrupeds: for every quadruped has its gall bladder in the interior of the belly, except this one. This animal, however, has its gall in its ears. And this animal's gall is like man's gall in heat; and this gall is very bitter and the cause of vehement anger and ferocity.

The ana is an animal of the East, as Aristotle says, naturally very fierce. Animals of this kind love one another with a wondrous affection; for if they see an animal of another kind approach one of them, all of them nearby rush together, and all attack the animal of the other kind with their teeth, and, having inflicted wounds, either force it to flee or kill it outright. For animals of this kind have large and long teeth; whence it happens that if by chance this animal is attacked by some animal stronger than itself, it frees itself and escapes by the very ferocity of its teeth.

The buffalo, as the Book of Properties says, is an animal larger and taller of body than the ox, black in color. It has long and twisted horns, a long neck, a huge head, lean limbs, a small tail, a gentle and simple appearance, but is of the utmost swiftness and cruelty when provoked to anger. It is most well-suited to human uses. It is possessed of the greatest strength.

As the Experimentator says, buffalo milk easily softens the bowels, heals fresh wounds, and helps those who have swallowed poison. The buffalo is patient of labor, has little hair, a terrible voice, a very rough forehead; it scatters earth with its foot. Its gall is medicinal, for it heals the scars of wounds; mixed with milk it soothes earaches. It has a very tough hide. A bronze ring with a cord is put through its nose, so that it may more easily submit to man for the work imposed on it; but if too heavy a load is placed on it beyond its will, it is at once thrown into a fury and lies down on the ground, nor is it easily forced to rise again by blows, unless the load that weighed on it is lightened.
This animal is called by another name, bison. The buffalo drags huge loads under water. Yet it breathes in the air with the strength of its breath.

The bonasus is an animal, as Solinus says, which has a bull's head, a horse's body and mane; but its horns are curved back upon themselves in such a manifold twist that if anyone should strike against them, he would not be wounded. When this animal is put to flight, it emits dung in a stream from its bowels behind it over the space of a full acre, whose burning scorches whatever it touches. With these weapons it drives off its pursuers. This animal signifies good prelates, who, having the austerity of life as it were horns in themselves, when they exercise it upon their subjects, do the least harm to them, because they show in themselves what they exhort others to do.
The camel is an unshapely animal, as James of Vitry says. Camels have two humps on their back and another on the chest, on which they rest. They have long legs, a long neck, a slow gait.

Solinus: as it walks, it never wears down its feet: for it has, as it were, fleshy footpads with a kind of reciprocating cushioning. Hence it suffers none of the wear that afflicts other walking creatures. They are kept for two kinds of service: some are suited to carrying burdens, others are swifter; but neither do the former take on more than a just weight, nor do the latter wish to go beyond their accustomed distances.
When they are to be loaded, as James says, they are struck lightly on the knees and immediately bend their legs and kneel down to receive their burdens.

Pliny: they are so roused by desire for offspring that they become fierce when they seek mating. They hate the horse kind. They can bear thirst for four days: but when the occasion to drink is given, they fill themselves so much that they both satisfy their past thirst and profit long into the future. They drink muddy water, as Pliny says, and flee clear water, or stir it into mud by continual trampling, so that it becomes turbid. And the reason is this: every element, the purer it is, the less it nourishes another element, and the more it is mixed with other elements, the more it nourishes; the camel shuns pure water, as an element of the earth, as if it were less nourishing when turbid, and seeks it out as if mixed, for the sake of nourishment.

Souls drink muddy waters when they seek the grace of the sciences that follow the understanding of the Scriptures, not those that are pure, that is, those which without allegory are fit for the angels alone.
[camels]

As the Experimentator says, rabies and gout afflict camels, from which they die very easily. They do not shed their hooves, but are most grievously burdened when they travel hard, long, and stony roads, for they have no shoes of stout leather on their feet.

Moreover the great Basil says of camels that they hold a tenacious memory of wrongs, and their rancor toward anger is heavy and persistent. And when one has been struck, having long concealed its pain, when it finds the opportunity, it at once repays the injury done to it.

Quickly swallowing the barley, they store it up, so that they may chew it again all night by rumination, says the Book of Properties. Camels are said to have this compassion, that if in a herd or stable one is held by sickness and does not eat, the others, as if sympathizing, abstain likewise.

Pliny: they last a hundred years, unless perhaps, transported to foreign lands, they contract diseases from the strangeness of a changed climate. They become stronger if kept from mating. There is also another kind of camel, which they call 'dromedaries,' vigorous with a wondrous speed of running. Camels carry their young for twelve months, beginning at three years of age. They give birth in springtime and again fill with young a year after birth. They mate facing away from each other. The male leaps upon the female and rides upon her the whole day through in mating. The male's member is sinewy and hard; and for this reason bowstrings are made from it. At mating time they seek out solitary or hidden places, nor is it possible to intervene without peril from the mating.

Those properly called camels have only one hump on their back; but those called dromedaries always have two humps on their back. Female camels have four teats, like cows. But male camels have their member set toward the rear, whence they mate facing away from each other. Aristotle: in each foot there is a knee, and above it the foot bends; and in each foot the pad is like the pad of a cow's foot, since it is small in proportion to the body. This animal is of an ugly appearance, and its feet are split into two, and behind each foot is a small fixed part, and between the cleft the skin is like that between the toes of a goose, and beneath its feet is much flesh. For this reason strong leather shoes are made for it when it must travel to a distant land, so that sickness may be kept from it, since change of climate greatly afflicts those already ill. These lack teeth in the upper jaw.
Pliny: the camel's brain, dried and taken as a drink with vinegar, calms epileptic fits, that is, the 'falling sickness.'

Dogs, as James says, are beasts trainable to every kind of game. And though they would gladly sleep, they nevertheless keep watch over their masters' dwellings by staying awake. They love their masters so much that they sometimes meet death for their sake. There is abundant proof of this fact. By barking at night they betray wrongdoers.

Ambrose: they say that at Antioch, in a remote part away from the crowds, a man was killed at dusk, who had a dog attached to him; but a certain soldier, driven by desire for plunder, had been the agent of the murder. Concealed by the darkness at the start of the day, he had withdrawn to other parts. The unburied corpse lay there, and a great crowd of onlookers stood by; the dog bewailed his master's misfortune with a tearful lament. And by chance the man who had committed the murder, as the cunning of the human mind goes, in order to establish his innocence by boldly moving among the crowd, approached that circle of the surrounding people and, as if grieving, came near the corpse. Then the dog, its lamentation of grief set aside for a moment, took up the boldness of vengeance and seized and held him fast, murmuring a pitiful song like some closing refrain. It thus turned everyone to tears, and lent credence to the accusation, for it held fast to this one man alone out of the many, and would not let go. Without delay that wicked man, since he could offer no defense, paid the fitting penalty for his crime. Ambrose relates this in his book on the Hexameron.

Pliny and Solinus report that, when Alexander the Great sought India, the king of Albania sent him a dog of unusual size. Delighted by its appearance, Alexander ordered bears to be released at it first, then boars, at whose contempt the dog lay motionless. The emperor, offended at the sluggishness of so great a body, ordered it killed. When the king of Albania who had sent it heard this, he sent another, equal to the first, commanding that it be tested against lions. Alexander did not delay, and the released lion was soon torn apart by the dog, which then, rising up against an elephant, killed it too.
[This is said] of the dog, that it recognizes thieves by scent, and distinguishes them from other men with an implacable hatred.

Solinus: dogs alone understand their own names; they remember roads. The Indians, at mating time, tie up female dogs in the forest glades, so that tigers may mate with them. But the first offspring from these, because of their excessive fierceness, are useless.

There are three kinds of dogs. The noblest of these are those of more elegant form, swifter for running and better suited to hunting. These do not know how to bark and, unless brought out to run, keep themselves within the house. They excel in the greatest speed, and are strong in the chest. These are called 'greyhounds.' There are also others suited to hunting, with long, hanging ears. These pursue the beast by scent and persistent barking and drive it to exhaustion, until they cast it down, worn out, upon the level ground before the hands of the hunters or the mouths of the noble dogs. These do not abandon the beast which they have begun to pursue at the hunters' command, even if they come upon many others; and this is what the Apostle counsels: that we remain in the calling to which we were called. Whence Jacob went on the journey he had begun, and the angels of God met him. The third kind of these is that given commonly to all for guarding; and though these are more rustic than the others, they are more suited to the services of men. In this kind there are manifold species: for among these there are large and strong ones, there are middling ones, and there are small ones, and there are the tiniest lap-dogs, which noble ladies carry in their bosoms. All these guard houses with barking and are hostile to strangers.
Pliny: their onslaught and ferocity are calmed, as Pliny says, by a man falling to the ground.
James: when they lie beside their masters' tables, they arrange themselves so that with one eye they watch their master's generous hand, and with the other they can see the door of the house.

Pliny: dogs bear their puppies blind, and carry them for sixty days. Their puppies begin to breed in the eighth month. It is thought a portent if a dog bears only one puppy. Females begin at six months. Dogs live sometimes fifteen years, sometimes twenty. From the twelfth year they cease to breed. During mating they remain joined together, and this is said to arise from the excessive heat of their lust. The best of the litter is the one that begins to see last, or the one the mother carries first to the den. For all dogs generally are born blind and remain blind for twelve days, though some for three months. The rabies of dogs is calmed by chicken dung mixed with their food. The root of the wild rose remedies their bite: for the bite of a rabid dog is deadly.

The greyhound, as Aristotle says, mates at the age of eight months, and some dogs do this: they begin to lift a leg to urinate. The milk of dogs is thicker than any other milk, except that of the sow and the hare; they have milk in their teats for seven days before giving birth. When one dog is hurt and cries out, the other dogs, indignant, attack it with their teeth. Dogs, in urinating, lift a leg and smell their own urine, because some of their urine is at times of a pleasant odor, and this animal is much affected by pleasant smell, especially in the sweet-smelling urine of dogs, and so they smell each other's hindquarters in turn. It happens to greyhounds that they can leap better after exertion than at rest. A male greyhound can live ten years, a female twelve. And it should be noted that in every kind of animal the males live longer than the females, except in the kind of greyhound dogs, and this because of their exertion. The lifespan of other dogs is determined as above. Dogs, when they are sick, as Aristotle says, eat the taste of a certain very foul-smelling herb, so that they may vomit up the noxious humors and be healed. Aristotle: the age of dogs is not easily known except by their teeth, for those of the young are white and sharp, those of the old black and blunt.

Very many have said that a dog cannot live except among men, and that it is driven mad if it is outside human habitation. The dog's tongue is medicinal, and by licking heals its own wounds or those of others. But if it cannot reach its own wound with its tongue, it licks its paw and, having anointed it with the medicine of its saliva, applies it to the wound, being certain indeed of the remedy which the nature of its tongue has bestowed. There are also other beasts which, like the dog, wear down their tongue by licking, whose saliva, if it touches blood on the tongue, brings on rabies.
As the great Basil says, in a puppy the teeth are not yet formed, and yet, when attacked, it tries to defend itself with its mouth.
As the Book of Kyranides says, if a nursing puppy often lies upon the chest of one suffering a chronic illness, the puppy will die and the chronically ill man will recover.

Male dogs do not easily harm female dogs; and this happens likewise in many kinds of beasts, God ordaining it thus providently even among brute creatures, so as to show that among rational equals there ought to be concord, and that the male sex should spare the weaker sex, if it were reckoned by the just name of man. It is a most unworthy habit of dogs to foully defile the loveliest and most verdant places. Shoes made of dog hide, worn on the feet, heal arthritic pain. Yet if dogs come upon them by scent, they will urinate on them.

Beavers, as James and Solinus say, are named from castrating. Their testicles, called castoreum, are useful for medicine. Because of these, when pursued by hunters, they castrate themselves by biting. Once the hunter has gathered these, he lets the beast go. But if it is afterward pursued by other hunters, broken by despair of escape, it rises up and, showing that they are already cut off, displays its severed parts to the hunter. The Poles say this is false of the beavers found among them, because the beaver's testicles do not project outward, but lie inside the belly like kidneys, and it excretes as a goose does.

Likewise it vomits up its gall, as Pliny says, which is useful for many medicines; for it is believed that this too is why it is pursued. Its rennet calms the falling sickness. It fells trees near a river as if with an axe. This animal cannot survive long unless it keeps its tail in the water, which is indeed similar to the tail of a fish.

As the Experimentator says, its tail has the taste and appearance of fish, whence it is eaten by Christians during fasting. Part of this tail is edible, part is forbidden for use; the rest of its body, however, is flesh. The beaver's tail, as has been said, is like the tail of fish, a cubit in length, having much fat.

Pliny: it builds its home, then, over the water, making various chambers within it, so that it may rise as the water rises or falls. The beaver feeds on the bitter leaves and bark of trees as its greatest delicacy. Whence it happens that its whole flesh, even if good, is nonetheless suffused with a bitter smell. This animal is most powerful in its bite, for once it has seized something, it does not let go until it feels that what it holds has cracked.

As the Experimentator says, beavers live in a colony, and go to the woods in large numbers, and, having gnawed off wood with their teeth, carry it to their dens in a wondrous manner. For they throw one of their number down on its back on the ground as a vehicle, with its feet raised, and skillfully arrange the cut wood between its legs, and thus, dragging it by the tail, bring it to their own dwellings. As the same Experimentator says, beavers do not do this injury to those beavers who were raised among them, but to those who came to them from foreign parts, and reduce these to servitude under strict guard. Others hold the opinion that beavers do this to those beavers who, worn out by old age and labor, have blunted teeth and can no longer cut wood either for eating or for building. Hunters recognize such beavers, reduced to servitude, by the wearing away of the fur on their backs, and, moved by pity, let them go unharmed. The same Experimentator relates a thing quite marvelous, if indeed it is true, I do not know: that they allow the otter (a small creature) to live with them in the water, and this only as the price of a service rendered, namely that in the winter season it stirs the water around their tails, lest the water, suddenly freezing, hold their tails fast in the ice and so trap them. If beavers have no otters to protect their tails, they look after themselves and descend into the water up to their loins, so that the water is not frozen by the intervening natural heat. They put the wood they have cut to a double use: they eat the bark, and from the wood itself they build very skillfully made dwellings. When about to eat the bark, it sits raised up on its hind feet, holding the wood with its front feet. It strips the bark by eating only that part of the wood which it held between its feet; what is outside its feet it discards and does not trouble with. Its hind feet are like a goose's, though larger and with claws, but its front feet are like a dog's; and in this nature is to be praised, which provided the beast with hind feet by which it might swim in the water like the duck, a bird, and front feet by which it might walk on land like a quadruped. When the beaver gnaws through a tree, having given it a blow with its teeth, it runs off at a distance from the tree, so as to avoid its fall if, once struck, it should fall; and it does this so long and so often, until by repeated blows it forces the tree to fall. The hunting of the beaver happens in this way: when hunters come to the beaver's dwelling, a dog trained for this is thrown into the water, which, reaching the opening of the dwelling, enters, and does not yield to the beaver's bites, until that skillfully made dwelling of the beaver is broken open by the hunters. This animal is shaped like a Pontic dog, that is, long and slender. It has very sharp teeth.
[It has] two above and two below, which are the same, as the Book of Kyranides says, with bony lips; and in this nature was provident, so that with these it might cut down trees most effectively.

[It has] a delicate and noble pelt, which is more precious the darker it is. It has colors in its fur like the badger's, but its hairs are fine and beautiful. Of this animal alone can the hairs on the pelt be gilded, and the eastern Saracens use them to adorn the head and weapons. Castoreum warms and dries, and has the property of thinning the humor of those who suffer spasms. It is most useful for tremors of the limbs arising from a defect of the sinews. The fat of the sacs of its testicles and of its groin is of great value for the aforesaid conditions. Wine boiled with castoreum, and the smell of castoreum itself kept near a man suffering from paralysis, is thus an incomparable remedy.

The chamia is a beast, as Pliny writes, which - as he also says - the Gauls call 'rufius.' This animal has the form of a wolf, and is sprinkled all over with the spots of leopards. In Ethiopia there is an abundance of these beasts, though they have been brought to foreign lands by men. The great Pompey was the first to bring this beast to the Roman games.

The calopus, as the Physiologus says, is a most fierce animal, so much so that it cannot even be approached by hunters. It has long horns shaped like a saw, so that it can fell tall trees by cutting them. When thirsty, it drinks at the river Euphrates. There is a shrub there called 'herychyna,' with fine and long slender branches. When the calopus comes and toys with it with its horns, its very horns become entangled in the branches, and, struggling long without being able to free itself, it cries out horribly. Hearing its voice, the hunter runs up and kills it as it lies caught fast.

The giraffe is a beast, as the Gloss says. It has a neck like a horse's, feet like a stag's, a head like a camel's, feet like a buffalo's, a ruddy sheen, sprinkled over with white spots. This animal is recorded to have been brought to Rome in Caesar's time. This beast is born in Ethiopia.

The goat, as is said in the Book of Properties, is a bearded animal, with long and sharp horns, and grazes in the valleys, on the mountains, and on the branches of trees which it can reach with its mouth.

It abounds in milk, and its milk is very wholesome, but as soon as it is curdled it spoils; for cheese made from it is of almost no use. As Aristotle says, in certain regions, after the first kidding, the goat's next pregnancy is not awaited, but her udder is rubbed with nettle. At first blood comes out, second something like matter; and afterward good milk, no worse than the milk of a pregnant goat. Goats sometimes bear twins, but quite rarely.

The billy-goat is a lustful animal, as Isidore says, and eager for mating; its eyes look sideways because of its lust. It sees equally by night as by day; and for this reason, if eaten, goat liver restores evening sight to those whom physicians call 'night-blind.'
Aristotle says, however, that they are often blinded during the day so that they do not see well by day. But at night their sight is sharpened.
As the Experimentator says, the gall of the billy-goat, applied to the eyelashes, destroys them.

For the same purpose, as the Book of Kyranides says, the blood of the billy-goat is effective, and it is a poison to all hair. The same book says that a fumigation from its hide rouses the lethargic and epileptic and is effective against suffocation.
It heals cloudiness and suffocations of the eyes.

If you place [something] of the billy-goat in some place, it makes frogs gather to it. Its burned hairs stop every flux. Its blood, if drunk, counteracts poisons that have been swallowed. Its fat heals bites and wounds. Its dung, if made into a poultice, heals toothache. Burnt goat horn, as the physicians say, if held before the nostrils of one who is truly epileptic, makes him fall at once. It also puts serpents to flight. The male among goats is called 'hircus'; it is a spirited, warlike, and robust animal. Its greatest strength is in its forehead and horns. Its blood, warm and freshly shed, has such power that it can break the adamant stone, which no metal can overcome.

Goats, as Pliny says, live on poisonous plants and do not die from them; but they say that if they swallow honey it kills them. A tuft of hair hangs from the chin of them all. If someone catches and drags one out of the herd by hand, the rest stand by, stupefied, watching. Their bite is fatal to a tree. By licking an olive tree they make it barren. Sometimes goats die from licking honey.

Aristotle relates something quite marvelous: a male goat was found in a certain region which, having teats, had milk drawn from them in such quantity that a whole cheese could be made from it. This billy-goat then mated with a she-goat and begot a male. Aristotle says this was not done naturally, but was a sign of some future event. It is nevertheless most certain that this same goat had the nature of both male and female, just as we can observe in hermaphrodite humans, who have both natures. It is nevertheless most rare, and perhaps unheard of, that one such creature should both beget as a male and conceive and bear young as a female. In Crete, when wild she-goats are struck by an arrow, they eat the herb pennyroyal so as to draw the arrow out of the body.

div.head: 19. De capra silvestri que et capreola dicitur

cit.quote: The wild she-goat, which is called 'capreola' or 'chamois,' as Pliny names it. It is a fierce beast toward its own kind, but toward other beasts timid and very gentle. On the island of Crete, a wild she-goat struck by an arrow seeks out pennyroyal, and having eaten it, the arrow leaps out of the body. There is much strife among the males because of the females, and this at mating time. This beast can scarcely be caught by dogs: for it is most swift. But it is caught in this way: when pressed by dogs on level ground, it flees to the highest mountains. Then the hunter pursues the fleeing beast and climbs up after it. When it has come to the very highest peaks of the highest mountains and has no place left to climb, and cannot easily descend, because by nature the descent is difficult for it and the ascent very easy, and it sees the hunter pressing upon it with his spear, it groans and, with tearful cries, appeals in a manner to the hunter, but in vain: for its groaning moves him to no pity, but with spear extended he casts it down from the peak among the rocky valleys and, once it has fallen, feasts on its flesh. It is also true that the chamois itself climbs to such peril for the sake of pasture that it cannot come down again; and then it is cast down from the heights either by hunger or by weariness of standing. But sometimes the hunter himself pursues the fleeing creature so incautiously that he too cannot come down, but dies along with the dying beast, and falls into the very danger he had prepared.

Cacus is a monstrous animal in Arcadia. This animal is entirely bristly like a pig; and, as the philosopher Aldhelm writes, it belches flames from its chest, that is, a fiery breath and spirit. It does this especially when moved to anger. But it may be asked how it can vomit flames or a fiery spirit from its mouth, and how these flames can be effective in burning what is nearby, without the animal's own body being consumed by the flames. We may answer that, while the breath is still diffused broadly through the many and various organs within the animal's body, it remains warm throughout without swelling into flame; but once belched forth, it is concentrated and multiplied against some object, receiving the power of burning, just as we see the light of the sun multiplied through the medium of a beryl stone, and, in the utmost concentration of the united rays, taking on the power of fire and becoming a violent fire upon the material beneath it.
Similar to these animals were those of which divine Scripture testifies in the book of Wisdom, that they would breathe fire from their mouths.

The monster Cacus dwells in caves above the river Tiber. This animal suddenly attacks herds of cows and bulls, nor is one animal from the herd enough for it, but, having seized three or four bulls by the tail, it drags them by the force of its strength into its cave, secretly, walking backward, so that it cannot easily be tracked. But this animal is not only hostile to animals, but also lies in wait most gravely for man himself, even though it greatly fears man.

Cacus signifies certain wrathful men, who indeed seem at first to grow angry only a little within themselves, but when, as their anger grows, they cannot restrain themselves, they belch forth, as it were flames, insults and reproaches upon their neighbor, to such a degree that they inflame not only themselves but also many others, overcome with them by hatred through their anger. And thus, by occasion of their wickedness, they drag many into the gates of hell, and this by a backward step, because no anger can be right or just. The wrathful man, therefore, is hostile not only to brutish men, provoking them to wrath, but also sometimes to rational and religious men, for indeed he is very perfect whom anger never casts down.
The cefusa is a monster, as Solinus says, which was brought to Rome in Caesar's time. Its hind legs and even its tracks resembled human limbs, but its front feet resembled human hands.

This signifies hypocrites, who, though they seem to have the outward marks of virtue and works, are within full of deceit. Whence Paul said to one such man: "God shall strike you, you whitewashed wall!"

The stag is an animal of wondrous speed, having a forehead roughened by branching antlers. Solinus: (the growth of the antlers begins when the stag is two years old); the branches increase with age. This growth continues for six years. After that the antlers cannot become more numerous, but only larger. In castrated stags they never grow, but neither do they fall off.
Aristotle: no animal sheds its horns except the stag. The horns of all animals are hollow except the stag's, which are solid and have no cavity in them.

This animal glories in its antlers; and even sometimes when it does not yet have antlers, it nevertheless struts as if it had them on its brow, and threatens with weapons it has never yet possessed, as Ambrose says.

The teeth show old age, namely when few or none are found. When they feel themselves burdened by sickness or age, as Pliny says, they draw serpents from their holes with the breath of their nostrils, and, having devoured them, seek out a spring as the poison presses on them, and, thirsting, after they have drunk the water, they recover their youth.
Stags, as Augustine says, when they wish to cross a river for the sake of pasture, support their antlers one upon another's haunches; and after the first grows tired, the last takes its place.
You, then, O man, imitate the nature of this animal, which fulfills the apostolic command, who says: "Bear one another's burdens," and, he says, "supporting one another."

They seek the shore not by sight but by scent, as Solinus says. When pursued by dogs, they are less wary of paths worn by human tracks than of secret places. The males, when the appointed season has roused their desire, rage with the fury of lust.

Pliny: the females do not conceive before the rising of Arcturus, that is, at the end of August and the beginning of September. They separate themselves at the time of conception. Before giving birth they purge themselves with a certain herb called 'seselis,' which makes for an easier delivery from the womb.

Solinus: (meanwhile they bear twin young), which they carefully hide, and, once hidden among the thickets, they strike them with their hooves to teach them to lie still. When they have grown strong enough for flight, they teach them the exercise of running and accustom them to leap over steep places. The flesh of fawns killed in the mother's womb effectively drives away poisons and heals the bites of serpents. When pursued by dogs, they are wary of the barking; and so they direct their course into the wind, so that the sounds fall behind with them. They are also wary of the whistling of pipes and every kind of music; and so, having sometimes escaped the barking of dogs, they follow after that same music, so that they fall again into danger a second time. With ears erect they hear most sharply, but with ears lowered they are said to hear nothing at all. Led by curiosity, they are astonished at everything; and for this reason they more easily present themselves in the way of archers.

As the Experimentator says, they are hunted by this device: two hunters go into a wood where there is an abundance of stags, and one whistles and sings, and a stag follows the music. And while it eagerly pursues the song, the other hunter shoots it with an arrow and kills it. Hunters have reported as a most certain finding that, when a stag reaches an advanced age, a bone beneath its eye is naturally pierced through, and wasps, formed and shaped within from a superfluous humor, or as others suppose from the marrow, emerge flying out; and then they say it cannot live much longer unless it is soon renewed according to what has been said above. They also say that these same clustered wasps sometimes emerge from the stag's nostrils.

They have discovered the herb dittany, as Ambrose says; for when they have been wounded by weapons, they eat this herb, so that, having received its power, they shake out the missiles. Ambrose says the same of the goat and other beasts. The same creatures, when struck by the phalangium, which is a kind of spider, heal themselves by eating crabs. The stag, too, when weighed down by sickness, chews the young shoots of the olive tree, as Ambrose says, and becomes healthy again. And it should be well noted that the blood of any animal that has a sinew coagulates, and if the sinew is removed, it does not coagulate, except very feebly and slightly, like milk in which no rennet has been put.

Solinus: they never suffer from fever. For this reason, ointments made from their marrow calm the fevers of ailing men. Also, continual eating of their flesh in the morning keeps one's life free from fevers. Their flesh is of greater strength and wholesomeness when they have been killed by a single blow.

The History of the Persians: Alexander the Great, to discover their lifespan, fastened open golden collars around the necks of many stags. These, captured after a hundred years, still showed no sign of old age.

They flee everything poisonous and detect it by a wondrous sense of smell. Whence the ancient hunters used to throw poisoned darts along the paths where stags had to pass. But the stags, sensing the poisoned darts, turned aside from them.

From stags' antlers, as Pliny says, the herbs celery and asparagus grow. The males, freed by desire for lust, eagerly seek out pasture. But when they feel themselves grown too fat, they seek hiding places, confessing the inconvenient burden. When they flee, they often stop, and this happens from an intestinal pain so severe that it can rupture within them at a light blow. Stags alone, every year at the appointed time of spring, shed their antlers, and for this reason they seek out the most trackless places and in that season graze by night.

For they flee wolves, knowing themselves deprived of their weapons. They seek out the sun, as Aristotle and Pliny say, and stand in it when their antlers are new, so that they may ripen and dry through the sun's heat and become strong. And afterward they go to trees and rub themselves there, testing their antlers; and then they go forth without fear, since they now have weapons. This has often been evident from little twigs of ivy clinging to their antlers. Having lost their antlers, they hide as if disarmed. And even in this good thing that they have, envious men deny that the right antler can be found useful for remedies. And so they shed their antlers in the water, so that they may be hidden there from human sight; whence the ancient proverb used to say: 'Go to the place where the stag has laid down its antlers.' A singular remedy for driving away serpents is the smell of burnt stag's horn.

Burnt and pulverized stag's horn, mixed into drinks, dries up all humors, as Aesculapius says. Likewise, powder of the same, rubbed on the teeth, strengthens them. The same powder, drunk with wine, heals epileptics, checks menstruation and flux of the bowels, and kills intestinal worms. If anyone wraps himself in stag's hide, he need not fear serpents. A stone is found in the stag's womb, and in its stomach or heart, which makes women conceive. Stag's marrow calms all pains of the limbs.

The stag has four teeth on one side of its mouth and four on the other, and with these it grinds its food. And it has other, larger teeth, which are larger in the male and smaller in the female, and their teeth curve downward.

Platearius: in the heart of the stag there is a certain bone, which serves as its support, as in other limbs. For on the left side there is a certain cavity, to which the spleen has a receptacle and into which it discharges its superfluities; these superfluities, through the dryness of heat, are changed into bony substance, and this bone is cartilaginous. This bone, extracted from the stag and hardened like bone, is pulverized and given to the sick for cardiac ailments and fainting.
The intestines of the stag are very foul-smelling, and Pliny supposes this is because it has gall in its intestines, which dogs abhor.

Some say that stags have their gall in the tail, others in the ear, as Aristotle says. For this reason they are not eaten by dogs, except when the dogs are famished. Hinds gladly give birth where wolves rarely come, and lead their newborn young to rocky places, where there is a single entrance to the den, so that they may fight more safely there against enemies. In its head there is a certain worm which almost constantly torments it. But every animal, and man himself, has a worm beneath the tongue. In that part of the body where the veins are near the vertebra joined to the head, there are twenty worms in number. Hunters say that if a stag, pursued by dogs, drinks water as it enters, it is refreshed from its weariness and restored for running. [It is also said that when it is weary and sees that it will be caught, it weeps, and, by a kind of presentiment of death, dreads the bitterness to come.] Stags fear the voice of foxes. Male stags fight among themselves, and the victor rules over many in a single pasture. The others, defeated, obey the victor with wondrous obedience, and keep peace among themselves, subject to one lord. When a fawn is captured by man and led a little while on a tether, it follows the man even when unbound.

As the Experimentator says, the flesh of the stag is melancholic and hard to digest. The fawn, which is the stag's offspring, has better flesh; and if the fawn is castrated, it will be even better, since it is more temperate in heat and moisture.

div.head: 23. De chimera, non illa que figmentum est, sed bestia a Iacobo dicitur

cit.quote: The chimera, as James says, is a beast found in the regions of Babylon, high in front and low behind. When this beast is captured, the Saracens offer it, covered with a precious cloak, to their lord, so as to serve him more agreeably.

It signifies those who offer their souls to demons through the cultivation and pomp of worldly glory. And there is no doubt that demons receive these gladly. Whence, in the Acts of the Apostles, Herod Agrippa, glorying in his royal robe, was struck by demons and gave up the ghost. And yet it is proper to kings to be clothed in purple and the noblest garments; but because he did not give the honor to God when honor was offered to him, he perished. What then, you poor, humble, and despised man, shall you receive for the glory of clothing and adornment, if you consider that not even a king glorying in the glory of his robe was spared?

The cyrogrillus is an animal forbidden by law. It is a small animal, naturally weak, and in this it is quite remarkable, that although weak, it is nevertheless hostile, rapacious, and deadly to other creatures of the earth.

The rabbit is a beast smaller than the hare, of nearly similar color and shape. This little beast, digging its dwelling in burrows underground, does the greatest damage to a vineyard, feeding on vines and crops by night. But in the morning, when it enters its burrow, it levels the mouth of the burrow with earth-dust from within, so that men coming upon it by day may not discover its dwelling. Wherever they live, they multiply excessively; for they give birth several times a year. When some rabbits sense something adverse in the place where they live, they flee elsewhere. Without delay the rest of their companions, disdaining the injury done to them, abandon the place along with them and flee. For they are of innumerable fecundity. As Pliny says: rabbits mate with their hindquarters facing each other, for their genital organ is placed to the rear. [When rabbits have gathered to graze, if one of them hears something suspicious, it strikes the ground with its foot, and then they all fall silent with heads lowered.]

The hamster, as the Book of Properties says, is a tiny animal in Apulia, the size of a titmouse. It has a head marked with white and black in different patches, is white on the belly, and reddish on the back. Its fur adheres so firmly to its skin that it could more easily be torn than plucked out. It digs its dwellings in the earth, from which it cannot easily be driven out, unless you pour boiling water into the burrows themselves.

And this animal signifies the miserly and the greedy, from whom indeed what they possess can be taken away by force, but who cannot be induced to distribute their surplus for Christ's sake. And the fact that it cannot be driven from the earth except by hot water signifies the miserly or the greedy, who can scarcely be recalled from earthly love unless some misfortune befalls them, which compels them to return to contempt of the world and love of God. Whence, when a certain despoiler of the poor had for the most part been cruelly stripped of his money by his lord, he restored to the despoiled what remained to him, and, converted, did penance before the Lord.
