The corocotta is a beast, as Solinus and James say, which imitates the voices of men like the hyena. It never closes its eyes. In its mouth there is no gum, but a single, perpetual tooth, which, so that it may never be blunted, closes naturally like a little case. It has such power that it can grind up anything at once. This beast is said to be conceived from a dog and a she-wolf.
It signifies scholars who always read curious things, but what they read is not truly wholesome.

So great is the power of their teeth that they mock whatever they see, or wish to penetrate whatever they hear from the Scriptures. These are born, that is, they are imitators of those who sometimes are wont to preach, and yet are wolves. Such men preach to their sons, saying: Why can we not be saved as they are? These sons of lions become young lions: they learn to seize prey and to devour men (Ezekiel 19).

The catoblepas is an animal by the spring called the Niger, as Pliny and Solinus write, dwelling around the banks of the river Nile, a small and sluggish beast. It bears its heavy head with difficulty, of so baleful an aspect that those who meet its eyes at once collapse and give up their life.
By this animal the lust of the eyes is noted; whence: "Whoever looks at a woman," etc.; whence: "David saw Bathsheba."

The dempna is a beast the size of a roe deer, quite robust and given to butting with its horns against beasts hostile to it. It is swift in running, keen of scent, and cautious of its life. Its horns, as Pliny says, are sharp, rough, longer than a cubit's measure, and raised upward and forward like the palm of a man's hand.
The fallow deer, or 'dammula,' is an animal, as Isidore says, so named because it flees from the hand.

As the Experimentator says, when the fallow deer gives birth, it immediately eats the afterbirth, before it falls to the ground. And the same Experimentator supposes that this afterbirth is a poison. For it is a timid and feeble animal; of which Martial says: the boar is feared for its tusk, horns defend the stag; what are we feeble fallow deer but prey?

These beasts signify poor and innocent men, who everywhere lie open as prey to the teeth of plunderers and princes. Or they signify those who, sluggish and cowardly in spirit, refuse to resist the devil, the tempter; and so demons rage against them at every hour with the various bites of vice: some in the head, that is, in the heart, through the mere consent to sin, others in the eyes, others in the tongue, others in works, through the hands of evil deeds, others in the ears, and others are wounded in the loins of lust, others in the feet of shameful desires through illicit loves.

The duran is an animal, as Aristotle says, cruel, swift, and very strong. When this animal is pursued by hunters and begins to be overcome by despair, seeing that it cannot escape, it hurls its dung violently, by a natural cunning, against the dogs pursuing it, and delays them with the stench of its putrid excrement. There have been some who said that this beast is the same as the unicorn; but no philosopher agrees on this.

The badger, as the Book of Properties says, is an animal the size of a fox. It has short legs, unequal on the left and right sides, but shorter on the left side. Whence it happens that, placing the feet of its right side in the ruts made by the wearing of cart-wheels, it can run vigorously and thus escape its pursuers. It has a shaggy pelt, stiff with white bristles mixed with black hairs. Its fat increases as the moon waxes and decreases as it wanes, to such a degree that if it is killed at the very end of the moon's waning, no fat at all is found. From its fat ointments are made, by which pains of the kidneys are eased and injuries of the limbs. And it is remarkable that, although this beast is medicinal on the one hand, its bite is nevertheless usually fatal and most severe (and the reason is this: for it lives on beetles and creatures which it digs up from the ground, which are venomous), and because venomous things infect its teeth, we believe its bite to be fatal, although even without venomous food, experience has shown that the teeth of wolves, foxes, and many animals are somewhat venomous. Whence the bites inflicted by wolves, foxes, and the bites of many animal-beasts are cauterized with a hot iron, lest the harmful bite bring on corruption. But venomous food, through the well-disposed nature of the internal organs, is transformed into excellent matter, and digestion expels what belongs to the poison and purges the rest, and transmits it, cleansed, into nourishment for the flesh. And for this reason it happens that the badger's fat is medicinal, but its bite fatal. This is even more clearly seen in the young of the viper, which lives on venomous creatures, and yet its flesh, made into theriac, is used against all poisons. We shall discuss this serpent more fully in the book On Serpents.

Of the badger these things hold true: anoint feverish patients with the fat of the badger, and they are healed. Its brain, well cooked with oil, calms all pains of the groin. Its blood, mixed with salt and smeared on the limbs, protects for three days from the plague of death. Its testicles, cooked with honey and eaten on an empty stomach, confer for three days the power of mating in those who are cold.
Elephants, as James says, are animals of great bodily strength and size.

For they have very large snouts, projecting ten cubits, like broad intestines made of tough cartilaginous flesh, which are called trunks, and which they use in place of hands, fit for every action, says Aristotle. And the elephant's nose is said to be strong and long; and no animal has this except the elephant alone.

And this is the reason, Ambrose says: since the elephant is taller than all other beasts, it cannot bend down to graze. Its neck, indeed, is smaller than the mass of so great a body would require, lest it too be more of a burden than of use. Through this same trunk the elephant takes food and delivers it to its mouth, and through it drinks and delivers drink to its mouth, and no animal does this except the elephant alone.

The Book of Properties: yet it does not taste or discern flavor with the trunk itself, of food or drink; and this is understood from the fact that, given wine, it draws it up with the trunk and pours it back into its mouth, and thus, sensing on the palate of its mouth the pleasure of the wine, expresses its gratitude with its mouth toward the one who gave it, caressing him.

James: elephants use this trunk in war, and with it seize men who oppose their side. They are warlike and exceedingly bold, especially when the blood of grapes or mulberries is shown to them in battle. The Persians and Indians are accustomed to fight riding upon them, carrying wooden towers with forty or fifty armed men upon their backs.

With an unbearable onslaught, as Ambrose says, they rush upon the enemy; so that they are checked by no battle-line, no massed ranks of soldiers, no wall of shields raised against them: they move through the battle like moving mountains, and, towering high like hills, disturb the confidence of all with the crash of their trumpeting. Alexander the Great - as is written in his letter - about to fight against the Indians, ordered bronze statues to be filled with burning coals; and the elephants, thinking those statues were men, stretched out their lips and were burned, and at once began to flee, both the men and the bronze images of men fleeing, none daring to touch them. On another occasion he overcame many elephants with the grunting and squealing of pigs together with the sound of trumpets, because they were not accustomed to such things. When an elephant is born, teeth already formed appear at once. But the large teeth do not appear in it until it grows older. These teeth are indeed two cubits in length and curve back from above. From these teeth, once burned, a powder is made which physicians call 'spodium.' This powder dries up bleeding of the nose, and is effective for cooling; it is given, with the juice of plantain, against flux of the bowels, of the menses, or of hemorrhoids.

The elephant's blood too, especially the male's, stops the flow of catarrh. The elephant, as Pliny says, has inside, for chewing, four teeth besides those which project - curved in the males, but straight and forward-pointing in the females. The elephant's tongue is small in proportion to its body. Its youth is known by the whiteness of its teeth: of which one is always in use, the other spared, lest, worn down by too much use, it be less vigorous should there be need to fight. When pressed in the hunt, they strike equally with both tusks, so that, one being ruined, the ivory need not be sought elsewhere. For indeed there is a special nobility in these, which is not found in the other bones of the body. When fighting together, they show no small care for the wounded, for they receive the tired and wounded into their midst.

And this is the hunting of elephants. The writing of the book that contains the accounts of the ancients relates that the elephant is captured in this way: two virgin maidens go naked into the desert, where elephants dwell; one of them carries an urn, the other a sword. When they sing in a loud voice, the elephant hears and hastens to them. As soon as it recognizes, by a natural instinct, the innocence of maidenly flesh, it venerates their chastity with the sweetness of love, and, licking their breasts and taking delight in their bosoms, is wondrously dissolved into sleep. Without delay the maiden with the sword pierces its tender belly and lets flow the elephant's blood as it collapses, and the other maiden catches the spilled blood in the urn. With this blood royal purple is dyed; and it signifies the blood poured from Christ's side, which one of the maidens, the Synagogue, sheds, while the other, the Church, receives it in the urn of the chalice. The former, through this, is judged impious; the latter, through this, is redeemed as devout. Nor is it without reason that the tunic of the true Joseph, woven in the virgin's womb, is dyed with this blood, so that the bride may rightly answer those who ask: My beloved is white and ruddy, chosen out of thousands.

There is also another hunting of elephants, according to Aristotle: hunter-men ride upon tame elephants and seek out the wild ones in the lower deserts of India. When they find them, they order the tame elephants to pursue the wild ones and strike them, until they obey and, exhausted, stand still. Then the hunters mount the wild elephants and strike them, goading them with instruments resembling small shields, and move them thus to fear men. Their forefeet are bound until they grow tame. They grow tame more quickly than all other animals, nor is any animal so domesticated and obedient to men among all the wild beasts.
Solinus: for they have understanding on the level of human senses and excel in memory. Whence they readily receive instruction and moral discipline.
Many animals, as Aristotle says, retain memory of what they see or learn; and this is true of the memory of estimation. But man alone is possessed of discernment and has intellectual memory.

There is also another way in which the elephant is tamed. As the Gloss says, at first, when it is caught by the hunter, it is struck by him and afflicted with many blows. While the hunter is beating the elephant, another man comes who wishes to have it obedient to himself, and frees it from the hands of the one beating it. Without delay the elephant notices the one freeing it, and grows gentle in his hands, and, loving him and always recognizing him as its liberator, obeys him.

You, then, O man, who are you, that do not give thanks to your liberator Christ, the elephant's counterpart, and do not always obey his commands? He who delivered us, says the Apostle, from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of his glory. And David: I will love you, Lord, my strength. The Lord is my firmament, and my refuge, and my deliverer; and for this he adds, saying: I will call upon the Lord with praise, and I shall be saved from my enemies.

Solinus: accordingly, when elephants wish to drink, they seek out rivers in herds. Loving one another and walking in harmony, they applaud one another with such movements as they can, as if greeting each other. The oldest by birth leads the column, and the one next in age drives on those who follow. When about to cross a river, they send the smaller ones ahead, lest the larger ones, entering first, wear away the riverbed and make deep channels by treading down the shallows. Between these and dragons there is a lasting and constant discord. Serpents lie hidden in the high places of the paths along which elephants are accustomed to walk in herds, and, letting the first ones pass by, they approach those coming after, so that they can help those who went before them. First the dragons bind the elephant's feet with coils, but the elephant unties the knots with its trunk as if with a hand. Then they attack the eyes or nostrils, since these places are not defended by the trunk.

Dragons are so large, as Pliny says, that they can drain the elephant's blood entirely. But the drained elephants become dry and wither. And so, when the dragons have drunk their blood, the beasts collapse, and the dragons themselves, made drunk with blood, are crushed beneath the mass of the falling creatures. The chief cause of this combat is that the dragons, scorched with thirst, are refreshed by the cooler blood of the elephant. For this reason they never attack them except when heavy with drink, that is, when their veins are more fully filled. The dragons, then, lie in wait for elephants in this way: they mark the places where the dragons rest beneath rocks or trees, and, lying there, crush them with the mass of their bodies as they lie hidden. The elephant, moreover, crushes great walls with its bulk and knocks down great trees with its forehead.

As the Experimentator says, sometimes, finding a serpent in its path, it attacks it and, having seized it, tramples it underfoot until it kills it. The elephant is also greatly feared by wild bulls; nor is this a wonder, since it pursues them relentlessly.
In the forests of Mauritania, as Pliny says, there is a very great river called the Amilo. To this river, at the new moon, elephants descend and there solemnly purify themselves with water.
Aristotle: the females engage in mating at ten years, the males at five.
Solinus: they mate every two years, and no more than five days in the year. They mate only in hiding, never without modesty.

As Pliny says, they do not return to the herd's company until they have washed themselves in running water. They never fight over females: for they know no adultery. It is said that a female cannot conceive unless she eats the fruit of the mandrake. The female about to give birth enters a deep pool; for if the newborn fell on the ground, it would not be able to rise.
A certain gloss: they place their young on islands because of the dragons that lie in wait for them. Whence, when the female gives birth in the water itself, the male stands guard over her.

Aristotle: in the elephant's mating the female bends down and the male mounts upon her, and this happens in spring. After the female gives birth, she rests for three years. Once the female has conceived, she is not touched at all by the male, and carries in the womb for two years. The newborn young at birth is the size of a three-month-old calf.

Solinus said the elephant gives birth once. But in truth elephants give birth five or three times in their lifetime. The male member is like a horse's, but small and not proportionate to its body. And its testicles are not visible outside, but are within, near the kidneys; for this reason mating is quick. The female elephant has two breasts - like a woman - beneath the armpits; and the reason it has no more is that it bears only a single young; and the reason they are placed under the armpits is that this is the first place for breasts. The male elephant also has breasts like these, but they give no milk. There are two kinds of elephants; but greater size marks the nobler kind. They fear and flee mice, because they are troubled by their smell; they also refuse food touched by them.

And, as Ambrose says, I marvel no less at the mouse, because it is terrible to the elephant, than at the elephant, because it is tall and splendidly glorious; and indeed it is a marvel that the elephant, which is fearsome to bulls and horses, fears the mouse. God is wondrous in the heights, and wondrous also in the smallest things. For a certain prerogative has been granted by God to each creature, so that they are each supported by their own particular privileges.

Solinus says that elephants find palm fronds most pleasing as food. If one happens to devour a chameleon, it is poisoned, but is cured by feeding on wild olive. They are very tough on the back, softer on the belly. They have no bristling hair. By the smoke made from the elephant's groin and hairs, any venomous animals are put to flight. They live three hundred years. They are most intolerant of cold.

James: whence ivory, which is made from their bones, is cold and white. For if cloth is placed upon ivory, the cloth is not burned even when fire is applied above it, but the fire is quenched by the natural coldness of the ivory.
Once tamed, they worship the king and offer him a crown. Solinus: hearing a man's footstep behind them without having seen him first, they tremble and stop still for fear of ambush.
They are so merciful that when King Bocchus threw thirty bound men before them, he could never make them serve as instruments of another's cruelty.
Solinus: they do no harm unless provoked. They kill flies settling on their back by contracting their skin into wrinkles; this serves them in place of a tail's hair.

Aristotle: the elephant sits somewhat on its haunches, but nevertheless does not bend its hind feet - rather its whole hind legs remain fully extended, with the legs and front feet standing upright - and so it leans to the right or left side against a tree.

Ambrose: for it cannot bend its four feet because of the weight of its body, since it needed stiffer legs, by which, like columns, so great a mass of limbs could be supported. It bends its heel slightly, but the rest of its feet are stiff from top to bottom. When, then, they wish to sleep or rest, they lean against trees, which sometimes, as Ambrose says, overcome and bent by so great a body, break, and the elephant which had propped itself upon them falls down. But those elephants more experienced in dangers lean against trees which can never fall. Hunters who cut the trees against which elephants are accustomed to lean, propping them with certain supports so that they do not fall completely, lie in ambush, until the returning elephant falls together with the tree it leans on and is unable to rise. At its cries the other elephants generally come running, and since they cannot bend down to raise up their companion, they groan together and cry out and, as if sympathizing, mourn with the mourning one. But the young elephants, putting themselves beneath it as best they can (with their trunks), sometimes raise up the one that has fallen, and thus it is freed from the hunters' hands.
And this is the reason why, once fallen, they cannot rise: they have solid bones without joints; whence they cannot bend their legs and shins. In their youth, however, they can bend them.

Its bones are very large. Its flesh, however, is very scant in proportion to its body. Its legs are nearly equal in thickness, like tree-trunks, from the sole of the foot to the belly. As the Experimentator says, it bends its hind feet as a man does.

The elephant has round feet like an apple, yet has toes joined by a hidden joint, which are not split, and for this reason they have no claws at all. When the elephant walks, because of the weight of its body and the strength of its power, it presses its feet very deeply into the ground, so much so that it is dangerous for other animals, such as horses and bulls, to walk behind it. The left foot moves more easily in the elephant than the right; and this is contrary to every kind of animal except man. Aristotle: and it should be noted that, contrary to all land animals, its intestines are arranged and formed differently. For it has in its belly a coiled, shaggy intestine, which, if you saw it without examining it by hand, you would think it had ten stomachs. It has no other stomach. Its liver is four times larger than an ox's liver, and the rest of its intestines likewise, except the spleen, which is small in proportion to its body. Sometimes the elephant suffers from a swelling sickness, and because of this it cannot then void urine or dung. And if an elephant eats earth, it will die. Yet there are some elephants accustomed to eating earth who do not die from it; and in this it can be seen how powerful habit is, which seems to be, as it were, a second nature. The elephant also suffers pain of the joints, and a drink of cold water and grasses steeped in honey help it against this. Wind greatly harms elephants, and through it they contract illnesses. When the elephant suffers pain in its shoulders, roasted pork applied to the spot cures it. Some elephants drink oil, some do not. In those that drink oil, if there is iron in the belly, it will be drawn out by the drink of oil. Elephants naturally drink wine gladly. And when they cannot drink, it is a sign that they are sick; and then medicine must be given to them, by which they can be purged. This medicine must be given to them mixed with oil, and they will be cured. When the elephant trumpets, it trumpets through its mouth, without the nose, and its trumpeting comes with much force of breath. Sometimes, however, it happens that it trumpets partly through the nose; but then its trumpeting is not fearsome, but sweet as a flute. The elephant grows for forty years, and then it feels the cold and winter and the cold wind. This animal is very much a river-dweller, since in India, where they are born, they always live along the rivers. When it wishes to wander in the water, it submerges itself up to its added appendage, that is, the snout called the trunk, since this appendage remains above the surface of the water, and it breathes through it. And it cannot endure swimming long because of the excessive weight of its body.

div.head: 34. De equis et eorum diversis generibus

cit.quote: Horses, as Solinus says, are bred in nearly every part of the world; but those of especially good quality are those born in Scythia and Cappadocia. Among horses, the sharper and more spirited one plunges its nostrils deeper when drinking. Horses generally recognize their side's enemies in battle. They rejoice at the sound of the trumpet and glory in combats; some horses also rejoice at the music of pipes, and some are roused to a race by lit torches. The lust of mares is extinguished by shearing their manes.

Horses are roused to lust by smelling each other mouth to mouth. For they are stirred to mating by the glory of their manes, and this indeed is also found among women. A woman, then, who holds to a purpose of chastity should be shorn, and not let her shoulders, fit for human dignity, be defiled like the tails of cows in their fine arrangement. It happened that a certain king wished to have a foal from a beautiful mare and her own beautiful colt. He therefore, having covered the mare's face, allowed her colt to mount her for breeding. But when the colt had mounted and, the mare's face uncovered, recognized his mother, he fled and at once died of grief; and so a horse does not mount its own mother.
In Scythia, they say, foals are born conceived from the wind; but these never live beyond three years.

Mares, as Pliny says, sometimes miscarry when pregnant, if a wax candle is put out before their nostrils. The same thing could happen to delicate women. A mare is understood to be barren if she does not conceive at her first mating. The horse begins to mate at two years, some at three. But whatever it begets before three full years is weak; but what it begets after, is stronger and better, up to twenty years. The male, however, continues to mount until his thirtieth year,
[a variant repetition of the same account, with slight wording differences, follows in the source]

but the mare until her fortieth year. The male lives to thirty-five years, the mare to forty. They say the horse once lived to seventy years. Still today in Sicily they say horses live that long, namely those born there and in Persia.
[a further near-identical repetition follows in the source]

The Gallic and Spanish horses live little, as Isidore says. Accordingly, in every animal that advances in age the teeth blacken, except in the horse, for as the horse advances in age its teeth whiten. Whence its age is discerned by its teeth. The horse has forty teeth in number, of which it loses the first two, on each side, at the thirtieth month from birth; the following year it loses as many more, next to those that fell.

Some say, however, that in our part of the world, as Pliny says, from the beginning of the fifth year it loses two, which grow back in the sixth year; in the seventh it has all its teeth grown back and unchanging. In horses especially, and in every kind of beast of burden, the ears show the signs of temperament: drooping in the tired, twitching in the fearful, pricked up in the enraged, relaxed in the sick.

In noble horses, as the ancients say, as Isidore says, four things are considered: form, beauty, worth, and color. Form, that the body be strong and solid, its height proportioned to its strength, its flank long, its haunches finally drawn in and round, its whole body knotted with the density of its muscles, its hoof dry and made solid with a concave horn. Beauty, that the head be small and lean, the skin close-clinging to the bones, the ears short and sharp, the eyes large, the nostrils wide, the neck upright, the mane and tail thick, the roundness of the hooves fixed with solidity. Worth, that it be altogether bold, quick of foot, with trembling limbs, which is a sign of strength: one that from utter stillness is easily roused, or, once roused to haste, is not held back with difficulty. The horse's movement is understood in its ears, its vigor in its trembling limbs. Color is to be especially observed here: black is best, and reddish or grey, white too is generally good; the other colors are judged inferior to these.

As the Experimentator says, Spanish and Gallic horses have a shorter life; but Persian, Epirote, Sicilian, and Dacian horses are long-lived. There are three kinds of horses: one of them is warlike, another suited to draft and riding, another suited to the plough.
Solinus: some horses are found who obeyed only their first riders, such as Caesar's horse, and the horse of the king of the Scythians.

The History of the Persians: also the horse of Alexander of Macedon, which, on its death, on account of its dignity, received royal funeral rites; in whose honor Alexander founded a city, which he named Bucephala in memory of its name.
Solinus and Pliny: there were also horses who, on losing the riders they loved, brought death upon themselves by starvation. Many horses shed tears when their masters are killed or die.

Isidore says that the horse alone besides man weeps and feels the emotion of grief. And men are accustomed to draw omens of a future battle from the sadness or eagerness of their horses. But these traits are found only in the noblest breed of horses. Those, however, that are not of this nobility give no proof of such goodness. Among animals, the horse, the cow, and the stag alone have cartilaginous bones in the heart, and this because of their great size, so that the heart may be supported by these bones, as happens in other limbs. But the stag's bone alone is medicinal, while the horse's or the cow's is not at all. Mares have such great affection that if one of them dies in the herd, another mare will nurse the dead mare's foal as her own. [When a horse is born, a small growth is seen on its forehead, and this is a most potent poison: it kills at once; but the mother mare, by licking it, destroys it immediately after birth.] For horses naturally love their own kind above other beasts.

The equicervus, as Solinus says, is an animal of the East, or of Greece. The hairs of its neck are like a horse's, hanging down over its shoulders. It has hairs beneath the neck near the throat, resembling a beard. The male also has horns, but the female lacks horns. Its feet have hoof-soles; its body is the size of a stag's.

The eale, as Solinus says, is a beast like a horse, with an elephant's tail, black in color, with boar-like jaws, bearing horns longer than a cubit's measure, useful for accommodating any movement it wishes to make.

For they are not fixed, as James says, but move as the use of fighting requires; when it fights, it extends one horn and folds back the other, so that if perhaps one is blunted or damaged, the other may take its place. This animal delights in the waters of rivers.

The henichires is an animal in the regions of the East, as Aristotle says; it is the size of a bull, and somewhat resembles it, but long hairs are found on it hanging down to both shoulders as on a horse; and these hairs are softer and shorter than a horse's hairs. And the color of its body is between black and red, but leaning more toward black. Accordingly the hairs on its other limbs resemble wool. The voice of this animal is like a bull's, and its horns are much curved back and suited for fighting. The hairs of its forehead are, as it were, shaggy, parted on either side above the eyes. It lacks upper teeth like the bull. On its legs the hair is sparse, and it has horny coverings on its feet; and its tail is short in proportion to its body. It digs the earth. And it has a very tough hide, enduring many blows. Its flesh is most sweet, and for this reason it is pursued by hunters. And while pursued, it flees, and sometimes stops and rests, and, when weakened, fights, and in the fight ejects its dung to a distance of four paces, and this out of fear. It is indeed an animal of much dung. When the time of this animal's giving birth approaches, many animals of its kind gather around it, and each, discharging its dung, piles it up like a wall around the animal.

The hemtra, as the Book of Properties says, is a rather small animal found in the regions of Germany. The male and female gather food in summer, on which to live through the winter. They make heaps of this food and store it in the ground. The female is naturally eager and lavish in taking food. The male, on the contrary, is sparing and miserly to an excessive degree, so much so that he scarcely wishes to spend even the thinnest sustenance on himself. The male, knowing the female's greediness, blocks the entrance by which she might reach the hidden food. But the female is naturally cunning: eager as she is, she makes for herself a hidden hole on the other side, opposite the blocked entrance, through which she can, unbeknownst to the male, steal enough for her greed. From this it happens that the sparing male wastes away in leanness as summer approaches, while, on the contrary, the female, sated, glows ruddy with fat.

The hedgehog, as the Gloss says, on the very passage where the law forbids unclean animals, is called by another name 'cirogrillus.' It is a spiny animal having the form of a little pig. Except on the belly, it is entirely covered with spines against ambush. For as soon as it senses anything, it first rises up, then, curled into a ball, gathers itself up into its own weapons.

Whence it happens that it presents itself with difficulty to be seen or touched, but this is overcome by a certain trick. The Book of Properties: it is put into warm water, in which, at once delighted, it relaxes into a full spreading out and display of its limbs, and so can be seen and touched unharmed.

Naturally foreseeing the future, it makes two breathing-holes, so that when it perceives the north wind about to blow, it blocks the northern one. But when it perceives the cloudy air clearing, it moves to the northern one, so as to avoid the harmful gusts from the opposite direction: Ambrose relates this in the Hexameron.

The hedgehog, as Aristotle says, hears more dully than any animal with a shell on its head; for the sound is heard through the resonance produced within the shell. For the hedgehog's nature is intermediate, as Aristotle says, between the nature of soft-shelled creatures - that is, the crab - and hard-shelled ones - that is, the hare and creatures like these. The hedgehog has five teeth, and between them a fleshy member. It uses its spines in place of weapons, as the ox uses its horns.

The Experimentator says that the nourishment of the hedgehog's body turns into spines because of the scantness of its heat, and, because the food is not digested, much superfluity is generated in their bodies; whence spines as hard as stones are generated, and this because of the great cold. The flesh of the hedgehog has a drying and dissolving power; it properly strengthens the stomach, loosens the bowels, and provokes urine; it is useful for those disposed toward elephantiasis. The hedgehog is fat and medicinal. Skinned, it resembles a little pig.

The hedgehog has two anuses, through which it discharges its waste. All quadrupeds that generate their young have testicles in the front part, except the hedgehog, whose testicles are near the kidneys, as in birds. Pliny: when it is hunted and, despairing of escape, becomes exhausted, it releases upon itself a wasting urine, so harmful to its back and spines that even if it escapes, once its spines are putrefied, it can scarcely survive. Knowing this, hunters begin to pursue it after it has urinated in the morning. In antiquity, garments used to be adorned with its spines.

Isidore: its cleverness is also such as this: at the time of the grape harvest it climbs the vine and strips off its grapes, so that the clusters fall to the ground. Having gathered these together, it rolls itself over them. Then, with the clusters fixed on its spines, it carries them off to its young. It is said to do this also with the fruit of trees.
The ash of burnt hedgehog, mixed with liquefied pitch, restores hair to a scar, as Pliny says.

Aristotle: the hedgehog mates with the female standing, joined and united face to face, and this because of the sharp points of the spines on its back; for if they mated back to back, they would prick each other with their spines; behold, then, the marvel of nature, which provides a convenience for each creature.

The ermine is said to be a small beast of the weasel kind, but smaller in form and different in color. In winter it turns white as snow, except for the tip of the tail. In summer, however, it is white only on the belly, while on the back it appears dark. It hunts mice; it feeds on flesh. Human vanity, in the height of extravagance, is accustomed to use the pelts of these little beasts on garments.

The falena is an animal born in the remote parts of the world, given and created for the punishment and vengeance of proud men. For this animal, by a certain natural indignation, detests pride in man, and, if it has the occasion to encounter him, presses steadily into combat and, victorious over pride, strives mercilessly to tear the man apart. But conversely, if it perceives in the man it meets a sign of humility through flight and fear, it sometimes stops and lets him escape.

The ferret is an animal which we commonly call 'furetum.' Its color is between white and boxwood, a little larger than the weasel, very similar to the polecat. It is thus a spirited animal, and excessively fierce beyond what nature grants it in strength. Ferrets are trained for this purpose, that they be sent into the burrows in which rabbits hide from hunters. And they boldly penetrate the holes and attack the little creature with their bites, until, driven out in distress, they force it into the nets. Nor do they hate only this beast, but attack whatever animal seems to breathe, however large, according to their strength. Nor indeed is this out of desire for flesh, which they do not eat, but from a will to do harm, or, as some say, for the blood of beasts, which they gladly take as drink. The ferret is fertile in offspring, bearing as many as seven or eight young at once. They are said to mate lying prostrate. If a female has no male, when aroused by desire, she swells up and dies. She carries in the womb for forty days. When the young are born, they are blind for forty days. From the time they begin to see, up to another forty days, the young begin to hunt.

The polecat, as Aristotle says, is a lustful animal. It gorges itself on food, and because of this often runs into danger. It cannot last long, this excess of corruption preventing it. This animal practices the act of lust with excessive intemperance: for lust follows excess in food. For its genital member is close to its belly, and because of the nearness of these organs, a nearness of vices often follows. When it mates, it is raised up and moves almost as if attacking, over the female; and when it cannot complete all that it intemperately desires, it cries out and is restless during mating. Indeed, in every animal, nature denies excessive mating, though the desire of lust may crave much. For seed is the power of the blood, violently ejected in the act of mating. Whence whoever exceeds the proper measure in mating is deprived of due strength and brings death upon himself before his time. For it is often heard that a man suddenly dies in the act of mating, and this because too ardent desire exhausts and destroys the vital spirits. This animal, the polecat, then, seems to mate in the manner of men: for the male is raised up above, and the female, lying beneath, is made equal under him. It never changes this order, though man himself, most disordered of all animals, changes the order of his own nature, mating from behind like a dog, or standing like the hedgehog, or with the female on top, which is the most shameful crime in every living creature: for no animal but man is found to do this.

The marten is a beast, as Pliny says, which, though small in body, is nevertheless of very great malice. This kind of beast dwells in a burrow dug in the ground. Lying in wait for animals in their dens, they cast out the excrement of their droppings and cover it with earth, lest passing creatures, recognizing the smell, know it as a sign of their presence. When, then, it sees animals passing by, it advances in silence, dragging its light footsteps with a heavy, careful gait. Without delay, when it sees prey conveniently placed for its mouth or claws, either it leaps unexpectedly and rages cruelly upon what it has seized.
By this beast are signified oppressors of the poor, who, as if casting out dung, confess to certain renowned and religious men, so as to appear good; and under this pretext they hide.

The finge are animals dwelling in Ethiopia. They have a dark color of hair, as Pliny says. Contrary to the custom of nearly all animals except man, they have twin breasts on the chest, with which they seem to suckle their young. They are animals neither too fierce nor entirely tame, since indeed they cannot easily bear injuries.
They keep peace with those who first keep peace with them.
The dormouse, as the Book of Properties says, is a small animal, varied in colors of white, black, and reddish.

Through the whole winter it sleeps and lies as if curled into a ball, and, in a marvelous way, as Isidore says, it grows fat from this very sleep. Meanwhile, with its vital spirit dormant, there is no movement, but this is remarkable: if you bring the sleeping animal out into the open air, it gradually revives, its breath growing stronger in the hands of those holding it.

It may be asked, then, how this happens. For it is impossible for an animal to live without breath, if indeed breath is called the drawing in of air, hidden or manifest, for the tempering of its innate heat. And yet that little spark of heat is so slight that it needs kindling rather than tempering. Whence for such animals the air alone, seeping in through the pores, suffices. For this same reason, no food at all is taken by them, because their sluggish heat would rather be smothered by it than digest it. And there is another reason: where nothing is lost, of necessity nothing needs to be restored. But in these creatures no wasting of the limbs occurs, whether from external, airy heat or internal heat. Whence no restoration is necessary. This same reasoning applies to the stork, which, being extremely cold-natured, in winter seeks out, at times, the places suited to its own composition, namely waters, and immerses itself in them, and, gripped by cold, lies as if half dead. Afterward, when the warmth of the season returns, it is naturally revived and comes out of the waters, and, washing itself of the mud, returns to the use of life. Having reasoned through these matters, let us proceed further to treat of the nature of the dormouse.

And so, as the season of spring begins, when the sun sends forth its warm rays, the animal, by its natural custom, returns to vigor. [Another reason why it can live without food in winter is this: that the animal is very cold and has little heat, and thick humors, which cannot be consumed by the vapor of so small a fire.] It runs in the trees as on the ground, and delights eagerly in the juice of fruits.
Pliny says that a decoction of dormouse, and the limbs anointed from it, will benefit those who fear paralysis.

The genet, as Aristotle says, is an animal of great boldness: it fights with serpents, and, once it has overcome them, eats them, and soon afterward eats rue, which is harmful to serpents. But the chief reason it fights with serpents is that this kind of serpent lives on the flesh of mice, and the genet itself gladly eats mice; therefore it pursues serpents as, in a sense, rivals for its food. This animal makes the entrance to its den from the north or south side, so that it is not troubled by a wind blowing against it.

The genetha is a beast a little larger than a small fox. It has a color between black and saffron, with black spots at times arranged in order on its pelt. It is a fairly gentle beast, unless provoked by injuries from other beasts. It does not climb to high places nor exalt itself in wonders above its station, but walks gladly among lowly places and along the banks of streams, and there seeks its food when hungry.

The guessules, or 'roserula' as it is commonly called, is an animal frequently dwelling near waters. It is larger than the weasel and smaller than the titmouse. On its back it is somewhat reddish, on its belly white. It makes its dwelling in the ground. It excretes a dung of a very fragrant odor, similar in smell to musk, though inferior in strength and intensity of scent. And this is remarkable in the beast: it heaps its dung in one place, as if unwilling to withhold it from man, but sets down its good thing ready for all to take. It flees the sight of men; by which indeed we are shown that, in doing good, we should avoid the sight and praise of men.

bibl.author: Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni Gregorius Magnus

cit.quote: Ibexes are beasts which, as the blessed Gregory says in the Moralia, are small of body. They dwell among rocks and there bear their young. And when, having horns, they sense danger threatening, they hurl themselves from the cliffs and land upon their horns; and thus they remain unharmed by any injury.
These, Pliny says, are of wondrous swiftness and are burdened on the head with vast horns. It is called 'ibex' in the nominative.

bibl.author: Historia scholastica Petri Comestoris Petrus Comestor

cit.quote: The Master says in the Scholastic History that this beast is of the kind of stags.
The ibex is an animal, the ibis a bird, and the envious ibis (namely from 'eo, is, it' [to go]).

The hybrid is a two-parented quadruped animal, that is, born of different kinds, as Isidore says. Just as the mule is born from the horse and the ass, so the hybrid is born from wild boars and domestic pigs. The 'titurus' is born from the sheep and the billy-goat, and the 'musmo' is born from the she-goat and the ram. When such crossbreedings of animals occur, the loins and hindquarters of the females are covered, so that the males do not avoid them because of their different kind.

div.head: 52. De istrice qui et porcus spinosus dicitur

cit.quote: The porcupine, as Solinus says, is a beast commonly called among us 'porcus spinosus' [spiny pig]. This animal dwells near the sea; but sometimes in the caverns of mountains, namely when it has no refuge near the sea.

As Pliny says, it comes forth in the winter months, and hides in summer. It is capable both on land and in water. This beast's back is bristling with quills, which, often loosed by a voluntary discharge, may wound dogs or men who come near.
For its anger, as James says, is very swift to take vengeance.

By these are signified heretics, who come forth in time of persecution of the Church; but when the Church has peace, they lie hidden in secret. They lie in wait to plunder the poor man, who lacks the gold of faith. They are bristling with the sharp arguments of their heresies, by which they kill those who come near them.

The hyena, as Pliny and Solinus say, is an animal that always dwells among the tombs of the dead. It has two natures: male and female. Its spine is so rigid that its neck cannot bend in continuous unity, except by turning the whole body around.

It follows the stables of horses, as James and Aristotle say, and by constant listening learns a name it can pronounce by imitating the human voice, so as to kill a man lured out by this cunning deceit. It also mimics human vomiting with false retching sounds, and in this way devours dogs it has lured. Hunting dogs, too, if while following it they touch its shadow, lose their voice and cannot bark. It changes its color when it wishes. Whatever animal it has once circled, that animal is fixed to the spot, unable to move. This beast carries a precious gem in its eyes, or, as some say, in its forehead. The hyena is the size of a wolf, and on its neck there are hairs like those on the neck of horses, and it has stiff hairs along its whole spine.
As Pliny says, hyenas are born in great numbers in Africa.

The lion, as James and Solinus say, is said to be the king of the animals. The kind of lions is divided into three: some are short and have curly manes, but these are cowardly and feeble. There are also lions bred from leopards, but these are ignoble and degenerate, and lack manes. But those lions that are taller and have a smooth mane are noble and fierce; they are free of guile and suspicion, and do not look sideways, nor do they wish to be looked at in that manner. The lion's temperament is shown by its forehead and tail. Its strength lies in its chest, its forefeet, and its tail, but its firmness lies in its chest.

They are of so hot a nature that they are said to mate at every season. The lioness in her first conception rears five cubs, in the second four, in the third three, in the fourth two, and in the fifth only one; after that she remains barren. And this is the reason she ceases to bear: because, as Aristotle says, the seed in the lioness is diminished by the preceding generation of cubs, which occurs in the greatest natural heat, more so in the lion than in other animals. And for this reason its nature is more solid and stronger than that of all animals, in proportion to the size of its body. The lioness has only two breasts, on the chest, namely in the middle of the belly, and these are small, not proportionate to the size of her body. And the reason for this is not that she is the mother of few young, but that she has little milk. Since food turns into body substance, and since she eats only rarely, and eats only flesh, which does not easily turn into the substance of flesh.
Augustine: when she gives birth, the cub is said to sleep for three days, until, trembling at the roar of the approaching father, it is roused.

And this is the reason why it is born as if dead: the lion is a most dry animal, whose dryness's violence thickens the moisture of the brain and makes it viscous. When, then, the openings and origins of the nerves, through which the animal spirit must be transmitted to the instruments of the senses, are blocked by this viscosity, the animal, though it has been given life, lies as if dead, because, its spirit being impeded, it has neither sensation nor movement. And although there is strong heat in it, since it is a very hot animal, yet because of the excessive dissipation of heat's effect through the pores in the mother's womb, the heat is weakened, so that it cannot dissolve the viscous humor and open the passages of the nerves. Coming forth from the womb, then, its pores are constricted by the coldness of the air, and the heat within is strengthened. On the first and second day, the heat begins to act upon the humor, to dissolve it; but on the third day, since the animal is most hot, from the movement of the choler, which makes its third assault, the heat is most fully strengthened. But when the father lion, whose nature is exceedingly hot, comes upon it, giving forth a mighty roar, the heat of his breath and spirit warms the air; which, by the force of the impulse and by likeness of nature, entering the ears and nostrils of the cub, cooperates with its natural heat, which, doubled - indeed tripled - opens the passages of the senses that were blocked by the humor, and at once movement and sensation are completed, and the animal is brought to life. But if it is asked whether the mother lioness can do the same for the cub, it is said that she cannot, because the lioness, by the nature of her sex being moister, would with her breath rather thicken the humors than dissolve them.

Solinus: the lion does not easily grow angry unless injured, but when provoked beyond measure, it utterly crushes its opponent; it spares those who lie prostrate, and lets captives who cross its path go free; it kills a man only in great hunger.
As the Book of Properties says, it rages more against men than against women, and this more against those who have known men than against boys or virgins.
When it sleeps, as Aldhelm says, its eyes remain watchful. When it walks, it covers its tracks with its tail, so that it is not detected by hunters.
As Pliny says, lions do not fight fiercely among themselves, but are peaceful with one another.

Solinus: when pressed by dogs in the hunt, it withdraws disdainfully and sometimes stops, and by this hesitant retreat conceals its fear. And it does this if pressed in open country. But in wooded places, as if unwilling to bear witness to its own cowardice, it withdraws by as swift a flight as it can. When it pursues prey, it aids its effort with a leap; but when it flees, it cannot leap.
Aristotle: alone among animals, along with the Arabian camel, it moves its right foot first, then the others.
Solinus: as it walks, it sheathes even the points of its claws within its body's coverings, like the cat, so that their sharpness is not blunted by wearing.

Aristotle: the lion lifts its leg like a dog when it urinates. When it opens its mouth, a strong odor comes from it. The lion, most swift for all its strength, is naturally sluggish, and this because of difficult digestion. When it runs, it strongly overshoots the limits of the course it intended, because it cannot restrain itself in its vehement rush. When it is hungry, it drags its tail along the ground in a wide circle, and, roaring, terrifies the animals, who do not dare to cross the path traced by its tail.

And it is remarkable, as Ambrose says: many animals, which could by their speed escape its attack, are so stunned and overcome, as if by force, by the sound of its roar that they collapse. The lion, proud by its very nature, in its ferocity does not know how to mix with the kinds of other wild beasts, but, like a certain king, disdains the company of the common creatures. It also disdains yesterday's food, and is averse even to the leftovers of its own meal.

So then, though the lion is fearsome to every beast, it is nevertheless troubled by the tiny sting of the scorpion, and wherever it sees one, it flees as if from an enemy of its life, says the Book of Properties.
They say the lion is destroyed by its own fury and consumed within by fiery blood, when its fury has no limit.
Solinus: therefore the lion, once caught by hunters, is terrified by hunting-spears. It fears the noise of wheels, but fire even more.
James: it also fears a white cock.

Pliny: the anger of a captured lion is calmed by this art: a cub is beaten before it, and it believes, by that example, that it too ought to fear the man whom it sees having power over the dog through such correction. Lions are never found fat or burdened with excess flesh. They take food or drink every other day, and also abstain further if digestion has not followed. Devouring more flesh than is proper, they drag it into their mouths, having inserted their claws into it. Indeed, when pursued and forced to flee even while sated, they do the same. The lion hunts the wild ass, and naturally hates it.
A sick lion, as Ambrose says, seeks out an ape to devour, so that it may be healed. A lion, having drunk dog's blood, cures its sickness by it.

Pliny relates that a man of Syracuse in Syria, when a lion, meeting him, rolled about before him suppliantly, was struck with terror; and when the lion, blocking his path on every side as he tried to flee, licked his footsteps like a flatterer, he noticed a wound in its paw, and, drawing out a splinter, freed it from its torment. In a similar way, a certain Elpis, a native of Samos, when he met a lion and fled to a tree, the lion at last, standing before him with open, howling mouth, showed the terrified man that a bone had lodged, caught fast, between its greedy teeth. Seeing this, he approached and removed the obstruction from the middle of its gaping mouth, and the lion, sensing that it had been cured by his hand, gave thanks, in a manner of speaking, by fawning upon him.

Females, as Solinus and Pliny say, have great desire for mating, and because of this the males grow angry. The lion detects, by scent, a mating in adultery with a leopard, and, so that his wrath does not fall upon her, the lioness washes herself in running water or keeps her distance for a while. Solinus and Pliny: its tail is still when it is fawning and gentle, which is rare; for anger is more frequent. It is also said to be consumed within by the heat of its wrath, when this is immoderate. At the start of its anger, its tail beats the ground; as its anger grows, it lashes its back, as if by a kind of goad. When wounded, it recognizes, by a wondrous discernment, the one who struck it, and singles him out however great the crowd; but the one who threw a weapon yet did not wound it, it seizes and hurls to the ground, but does not wound.

When it fights for its cubs, it fixes its gaze on the ground so as not to be frightened by the hunting-spears (Pliny). The lion's flesh, and especially its heart, gives warmth to those who eat it, and for this reason it is given as a remedy to those suffering from excessive cold. Its bones are of such hardness that fire is struck from them as from flint.

Aristotle: for its bones are especially hard and larger than the bones of other animals, and for this reason, when struck one against another, fire springs out. In these bones there is very little cavity, nor is there any marrow in them except very slightly, and this only in the bones of the hips and forearms.

As the Experimentator says, the lion's fat is a counter-poison. A man anointed with wine and lion's fat drives away all beasts; it also puts serpents to flight. Its fat is warmer than that of all quadrupeds. The lion nearly always suffers from fever, and this a quartan fever; and then it especially craves the flesh of the ape, so as to be healed. At its roar, all animals stop still, even those who have never seen or encountered it before, and this by the command of ruling nature; for nature has instilled in them a fear of the lion. When the lion walks over hard and stony ground, it spares its claws, as it were its own blades.

Pliny: lion's fat, mixed with rose oil, protects the face from blemishes and gives it a bright, healthy glow. The bone of its neck is a single continuous piece, and the flesh of its neck is cartilaginous and like a single sinew; whence it cannot bend its neck backward or to the side.
[a fragmentary entry on a bone of the lion]
Aristotle: its internal organs, indeed, in every way resemble those of the dog. Its teeth are like the dog's, though larger. Its molar teeth, however, are broader on the inside.
The leopard, as Solinus says, is an animal begotten from the lion and the panther. Of these, the females are bolder and stronger than the males.
Pliny: if anyone wishes to withstand a raging leopard, let him rub garlic between his hands, and without delay the leopard will draw back and not resist, because it cannot bear the smell of garlic.

Ambrose: the leopard, gripped by an internal sickness, drinks the blood of the wild she-goat, and thus escapes the force of its languor. The leopard has a reddish color, with spots of black all over. They are much smaller than lions. When the leopard eats something poisonous, it seeks out human excrement, which it eats, and is healed. Some believe the leopard and the panther are the same beast, but with different names. Ambrose: these beasts are naturally most cruel, whence it is said: If the Ethiopian can change his skin, or the leopard his spots - that is, the fickleness of his temper. They are sometimes tamed, but never so much that they forget their cruelty. They are, however, tamed for hunting. Thus when they are led out to the hunt, they are released after the prey. If it cannot be caught after four or five leaps, it stops, fiercely enraged. And unless the hunter immediately offers the raging beast some animal by whose blood it may be appeased, it rushes upon the hunter or whoever crosses its path, because it is impossible to calm it except with blood. But in this those who wish to hunt with these beasts are provident, in that they always keep lambs or other animals with them, with which to appease them when angry.

The lamia, as the Book of Properties says, is a large and most cruel animal. By night it comes out of the woods and enters gardens and breaks trees and scatters their branches, and this with arms that are exceedingly strong and fit for any action. But when men come upon it to stop it, it fights with them and bites them.
But this is most marvelous about its bite, as Aristotle relates: a man wounded by the lamia's teeth is not healed of the bite until he has heard the roaring beast's voice.
And indeed we do not know whether these are the lamias of which Jeremiah says in Lamentations: The lamias have bared their breast, they have suckled their young.

And indeed, according to the Gloss on this passage in Lamentations, it can well be believed, for the Gloss says, that this beast is most fierce, and yet gives its breasts to its young when they ask, and suckles the tender ones.

Jeremiah calls these beasts to the memory of the Jews and reproaches them for being crueler than the lamias themselves, since their little ones asked for bread and there was none to break it for them. This animal is called in Hebrew 'lidit,' and the Jews suspect it was one of the Furies, who are called the Fates, because they spare no one. I have heard from a certain man that lamias are beasts in the East, around those regions that contain the Tower of Babel in the plain of Shinar. And these beasts are larger than goats and are exceedingly rich in milk, and are tamed by men and led out to pasture, and are useful for their abundance of milk.

The lanzani is an animal, as Solinus and James say, most savage, from whose cruelty no beast can be safe. For, as they say, it even terrifies the lion itself, which is nevertheless reckoned fearsome to all. It preys upon beasts not of its own kind, but spares its own kind. It hunts down, with implacable hatred, those animals that prey upon other beasts. And though it pursues this crime in others, it is unmindful of its own iniquity. It pursues man in a wondrous way, and this perhaps by divine judgment, so that the creature that ought by nature to be the gentlest of all animals is, through the malice of its vicious wickedness, the most savage of all.
The lynx, as Pliny, James, and the Lapidary say, is a beast which has such piercing eyes that it is said to be able to penetrate solid bodies with the subtlety of its sight.

It is no small question, however, how this can be. It is established, according to the Philosopher, that the eye is situated in moisture. Now there are three things in water: watery moisture, transparency, and the keenness of light, and this last it shares with the celestial nature, and this is the ultimate purification from matter in the nature of light. And since light is the ultimate transparency in a bounded body, therefore if a watery substance is posited in its ultimate purification as regards transparency, then in the eye of the lynx it will be able to penetrate a solid and dark body. This too is found marvelous in its nature, that whatever it has seen, it forgets at once, as soon as it turns its eyes away.

As Pliny says: it bears only a single young at a time. The lynx has a tongue like a serpent's, though larger, which it extends to great length. It turns its neck around, and has large claws. Those who have studied this animal's nature more fully have said that its urine hardens into a precious stone. This stone is called 'ligurius.' But out of a certain natural spite, they hide the discharged liquid in the sand as much as they can, so that such an excretion may not pass into human use.
[a near-duplicate passage repeating the account of the lynx's penetrating sight, given twice in the source]

The wolf-dog is a beast in the regions of the East, which some place among the kind of wolves. It has a maned neck and is so varied that they say no color is lacking to it. It is longer than the wolf, but has shorter and dissimilar legs; this animal is swift in leaping; it lives by hunting; it is harmless to man. And this should be noted about this beast, that it changes its appearance according to the seasons, for in winter it is shaggy and bristling with hair, but in summer it is bare.

This animal signifies flatterers or slanderous subordinates, who, while their superiors are persecuting certain people, then, as it were, clothe themselves in bristling hair and rage against their fellows with a mind to do harm, and believe this to be honorable for themselves. But in time of peace they waste away with envy.
The wolf, as James says, is a most rapacious and deceitful animal.
Some have said that wolves are 'wild dogs': for its form is like that of dogs, its howl similar, but it lacks barking.

When it has seized a sheep, with the shepherd in pursuit, it does not harm the sheep with its teeth, but makes it lie gently upon its own back, lest, perhaps feeling hurt, the sheep struggle and delay the wolf's flight.

Ambrose: the man whom a wolf sees first falls silent, and, forestalled by the harmful creature's gaze, though he has the will to cry out, he has no service of voice; and the wolf despises him as the victor who has taken away his voice.

And this is the reason, as the Experimentator says: it sends the rays of its eyes into the man and dries up his visible spirit, which, once dried, dries the man's other spirits, and these in turn dry up the arteries, and so the man is made hoarse. It has a liver different from other animals, in the likeness of weapons.
As Aristotle says, near the sea they tear apart fishermen's nets set out to dry, unless the fishermen leave fish for them in the place.

The Experimentator: it gathers willow leaves in its mouth and hides beneath them, so as to secretly seize goats that come to the leaves. When the wolf walks among leaves, so as not to be detected by the sound, it licks its feet with its tongue, and thus makes them slippery and moist, so that it is not heard by dogs. The wolf's sight is dull by day, but it sees more clearly by night. Animals that see more clearly by night are generally dimmer of sight by day.
Pliny: if a wolf senses it has been seen beforehand by a man, it lays aside its ferocity, and no longer has the vigor of its usual speed in running.

Ambrose: if a wolf sees you first, it takes away your voice; and if you fall silent, loosen your cloak, so as to loosen your speech. If a wolf rises against you, seize a stone, and it flees; if it pursues you, going gradually behind your back to lie in wait for you, place some marker between you and it, in its sight, and, fearing entrapment, it will stop. And this same thing, against the devil, is the sign of the cross, that the attacker may cease.

Wolves mate throughout the whole year for no more than twelve days. Their members are bony. Only at the time when they mate do they go about in packs; and they howl together, with only one leading and the rest crying out in response, and at that time they are more fearsome and dangerous. In hunger they eat earth.

But then too, once burdened with this food, they seek to attack an ox, or a horse, or some such robust animal. For indeed, attacking it through the nostrils, when the animal tries to shake them off, it is worn down by this deceitful weight, and falls to the ground, overcome. Then, unburdening themselves of the earth they had eaten, they return to the prey. Wolves, when, after a long fast, they begin to eat flesh they have found, if by chance they catch sight of something else, they forget at once, and, forgetful of the abundance before them, go off to seek the satisfaction they had abandoned.

Pliny: they are said to divide their plunder among themselves in equal shares. In the wolf's bladder there grows a small stone called 'syrtites,' but only through the dire torment of certain men. The wolf does not grow fat, because it devours the food it eats without chewing it, so that it does not turn into nourishment for the body.

Ambrose: the wolf, when sick, eats earth and herbs as medicine; having eaten this, it vomits at once and is healed. For no flesh-eating animal eats herbs with impunity (except man and the bear); dogs do the same when they are sick.

Aristotle: it happens that wolves often fall sick, because they swallow much food without cutting or chewing it, and they go two days without food because of the digestion of their food. It lives on little water, and this because drink does not help undigested food. Its dung is dry, without any moisture, and comes out with difficulty, and with it comes a strong gas from the lower region; and its urine has a strong smell. It lifts its leg when it urinates, as dogs do. Wolves sometimes eat men, and this by chance: for it happens rarely. It is said, however, that this does not happen unless it has by some chance first eaten from the corpse of a slain man, which it happened to find lifeless in the fields. Then, having tasted the sweet food of human flesh, which is more delicate than all other flesh, it seeks again to eat, enticed by the sweetness of the flesh, and does not fear to fall into danger by attacking a man. [As long as the mother she-wolf lives, none of her daughters is thought to conceive or bear young. And this is quite plausible, for if they could conceive and bear young, the multiplication of wolves would become far too troublesome for other animals. And in this benevolently provident nature has shown great discernment. It has often been found that she-wolves have seized human infants, and nourished them for many years on raw flesh.] [In the forests of Burgundy, when nets were set for wolves by hunters, a captured female of sixteen years was caught, who, in a wondrous way, before falling into the hunters' hands, defended herself with her teeth. The palms of her hands were hardened with the firmness of calluses. She was carried most swiftly on her hands and feet with an exceedingly powerful gait. She lived long after her capture on raw flesh. She very often turned back toward the forests. She tried to speak, and later learned to: she said she had twice been made pregnant by a wolf, and twice, not having seen offspring like herself, devoured what she had borne. I have seen the man who reported having seen this woman, and I believe he was not lying in this.] When wolves flee, they carry their cubs with them, and, if caught by a hunter, leap up into trees they can reach with a jump, and hide among the branches, until the hunters have passed. When they come out of their dens, they eat dragon-arum and chew it with their teeth to sharpen their teeth. It is proper to wolves to fear fire. But when wolves grow old, they go to places near cities, so as to find prey more easily, since when old they can hunt only with great difficulty. The life of wolves is very long, and in old age they lose their teeth. Their internal organs are weak, and easily become corrupted in their wounds, and the rest of their body suffers many injuries. Its head is exceedingly strong, and the wounds that result from its bites or claws are very bad, since venom comes from them; and the same remedy applies to its bites as to the bite of a rabid dog. The dispositions of its soul are these: it is bold, and this more so in the kind that is short than in the kind that is long. It can be tamed without anger and kept among men with affection, and will play with them like a puppy. It will naturally flee hunters, and will not forget the perpetual hatred and cunning it had toward lambs and small animals, which it used to eat.
Wolves, as Isidore says, are nurtured by Ethiopia with maned necks, and so varied that they say no color is lacking to them.

A wolf passing through a hedge, as a certain book says, secretly lying in wait for sheep, if it happens to make a noise with its foot, immediately bites its foot as if it were guilty. The wolf buries surplus food in the ground. If it finds stray dogs and can catch them, it kills them and buries them in the ground.

Albert: likewise, not only the living wolf but even its dead carcass is so pursued by noble dogs that, even if its flesh is prepared in the most delicate way, they distinguish it from other meat by smell alone, and, turning away their gaping mouths, gnashing their teeth in excessive indignation, let out fierce barks against it.
Bishop John says: the cubs of wolves, though too weak to hunt, nevertheless delight in blood and play at biting.

A wolf entering a sheepfold kills all the sheep before it touches even one to eat. The wolf's brain is said to grow and shrink according to the phase of the moon; and this, though true in all quadrupeds, is more so in the wolf, except the dog, in which nature has granted the same. The wolf's heart, burnt and reduced to ash, given as a drink, is said to help epileptics, provided the patient is afterward stained by no lustful act. The wolf's heart, if dried and kept, is said to become very fragrant.
As the Experimentator says, the Ethiopian wolf has a neck maned like a horse's, and is of such variety that it is believed no color is lacking to it.

The wolf-dog hybrid is a quadruped animal, as the Experimentator says in his book, an animal from the mixture of dog and wolf; and this occurs with a she-wolf as mother and a dog as father. For both parents are so lustful that, though the natural hatred between dog and wolf opposes it, they nevertheless come together for mating for the sake of lustful pleasure. And so it happens that the offspring takes on the color and habits of both parents. These beasts are strong and very fierce.

They signify those who, from mere possession of knowledge, not of grace, usurp for themselves the office of preaching, and yet are wolves. Though they may indeed convert some from worldly life through preaching, they afterward do not fear to draw them back to sins and crimes; and to those to whom they ought to have been nourishers in the growth of grace, they become destroyers through a relapse into crimes. Whence Peter, the prince of shepherds, appearing to a certain priest who had for many years been given over to worldly deeds, said to him: You were putting to death souls that do not die. When, then, will you bring back from hell the souls you have handed over to punishment through your crime? And when, out of confusion, he could not answer, returning to himself from the vision he abandoned the world, and, devoted to the service of Christ, passed to Christ by a most blessed end. This the most holy and celebrated man, Master John of Nivelles, related many times, as one who, at the point of death, heard this same priest, to whom the divine revelation we have spoken of was made.

The leucrocota, as James and Pliny say, is a beast that surpasses all other beasts in speed. It has a body like an ass's, the haunches of a stag, the chest and legs of a lion, and the head of a camel, but with a mouth opening wide and vast, up to the ears. It has cloven hooves. In place of teeth it has a solid bone; and it imitates the voices of men.

The leoncophana, as Solinus and James say, is a small beast, which, once caught, is burned, so that the paths of lions may be sprinkled with its ash. For lions are killed if they touch even a little of it. For this reason lions pursue this beast with a natural hatred, and, once caught, tear it apart. But lions, in the very act of biting this beast, lose their life. And indeed, when the lion approaches, this creature also sprinkles its urine, knowing that this too is deadly to the lion.

This animal signifies humble souls, who, bound by the chains of religion, burn with love of God and neighbor. With whose ash - that is, the memory and example of their deeds - the paths of the proud ought to be sprinkled, so that, pricked by imitation of them, they may die to the world. But those, on the contrary, rendering evil for good, tear apart with slander and envy the good report they have heard of them. Let them know, too, that in this very act of slander, sinning mortally, they perish by their own malice and envy.
The lacta, as the Gloss says, is a small animal, likewise forbidden in the Law. It dwells more often among the tombs of the dead, and naturally delights properly only in these.
The hare, as the Book of Properties says, is a rather small beast. It excels in swiftness. Among other beasts it is the more timid, whence it rarely goes out to graze except by night.

It never grows fat, as Pliny attests. This little beast is said to play, in jest, with the weasel. And when the weasel sees the hare tired from play, it seizes its throat, once relaxed, with its teeth, and grips it most fiercely. Soon the hare, feeling the weasel's bite, tries to escape by speed, but, weighed down by the deceitful burden, even if it can wander a little, it is more from its own weariness than from any real escape. For the weight follows it as it flees. So it happens that, the hare falling from exhaustion, that wicked beast kills it by cunning treachery and eats it. Hares change their sex every year. Pliny: they do not grow fat. In the winter months they eat snow for food; and this is proven by the fact that after the snow they take on a ruddy hue.
Ambrose: in some parts of the world hares turn white in winter, and return to their original color in summer.
Pliny says that the hare has as many openings for excrement as it has years of age.

The hare, as the Experimentator says, at the time of the crops and the harvest, exults and is moved to play, as if speaking through its play, because a season of abundance is at hand, and so it is a time of joy, not of sorrow.

The hare's lung, applied to the eyes, heals them. Crushed and applied as a poultice, it heals injured feet. [Fresh hare's lung, as Aesculapius says, hung about the neck, removes quartan fevers and helps epileptics. Its gall clarifies the eyes. Its kidneys, dried, powdered, and drunk, expel a stone from the bladder. Its blood, drunk with warm water, does the same. Its womb, dried, powdered, and drunk together with its rennet, causes conception of a male. Its blood together with its rennet does the same.]
No animal having teeth on both sides of the jaw has rennet, except the hare. And the older it is, the better. It is effective against flux of the bowels.
[a near-duplicate repeats the same medicinal properties of fresh hare, as Aesculapius says]

As the great Basil says, its flesh generates thick blood; yet it is beneficial to those who have too much moisture. Its hind legs are longer, whence it happens that it is easier for it to climb a mountain than to descend. It does not ruminate. It sleeps with its eyes open. The great Basil says that the kind of hares is not easily wiped out wherever they begin to dwell, and this because they multiply beyond estimation, so that it may be said of them by a special grace: Be fruitful and multiply. If a hare is raised within the walls of a house among men and lacks its natural swift movement, a mass of fat grows over its kidneys, and it dies. For much movement in an animal diminishes the fatness that it could otherwise have gathered from much food. The hare, around the place where it must rest, leaps in a repeated zigzag, so as to deceive the sluggishness of hunters; and this can best be observed in time of snow.

Solinus: it was fitting that the hare, born as prey for all, should multiply beyond measure, and in this nature was kind, since it is almost the only animal that, bearing young, clothes one already with fur in the womb while carrying another without fur, and yet another still laid up in seed, all at the same time. In Ithaca, as Pliny says, hares brought there die, and this indeed on the outermost shores, just as in Africa boars, stags, goats, or bears do not live.

The otter, as the Book of Properties says, is a cunning and malicious animal, dwelling around ponds and rivers. It is the size of a cat, of nearly similar form except in the head. It is dusky and black in color, with a shining coat.

To it, as Pliny says, the fur is softer than down, and its sheen does not easily yield to age; whence trimmings are made from its pelt for the collars of men's and women's garments. This beast has dens above the waters, and burrows, in which it dwells and bears its young. It lives on fish and hunts them with wondrous frequency. Though it can live long under water, it nevertheless draws its breath from the air; whence it sometimes happens that, when it enters a fish-trap - that is, an instrument made of twigs for catching fish - for the sake of plunder, since it will not abandon its prey and cannot return by the way it entered, because the shape of the trap prevents this, and it cannot tear the instrument apart quickly enough, it must in the meantime be suffocated in the water, since it could not recover its breath in the air. Some call this instrument a 'weir.'
